When you think of Black Friday, there's a good chance your mind goes to waiting in long lines to grab doorbuster deals at your local Walmart store. While the shopping event has drastically transformed over the last decade, one thing still rings true in 2026: Walmart has one of the most anticipated Black Friday sales of the season.

Sources indicate that walmart is still where you go if you want to shop Black Friday deals in person and avoid shipping altogether. But the retailer also hosts a pretty epic online savings event each year. You'll find deals and discounts across practically every department in the lead-up to the holidays, with things coming to a head on Black Friday proper.

To help you get the details straight and gear up to shop at Walmart on Black Friday 2026, here's everything you need to know, including when stores open, the best deals already live, ad highlights, and how to get early access.

Black Friday officially takes place on Friday, Nov. 27 in 2026. However, most retailers will kick off their Black Friday sales before that. Walmart has announced prepares for three major holiday shopping events on its Black Friday 2026 calendar.

Recent findings suggest that walmart Early Black Friday Sale: Nov. 12 to Nov. 15.

Walmart Black Friday Sale: Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET to Nov. 29 (online only Nov. 23 to Nov. 26, in stores at 6 a.m. local time on Nov. 27).

According to recent reports, walmart Cyber Monday Sale: Nov. 30 at 12:01 a.m. ET to Dec. 2 (online only).

Industry observers note that walmart+ members have access to "hot deal drops" starting 12:01 a.m. ET on Nov. 23. According to the superstore, any remaining hot deal drops are open to all customers starting 12:01 a.m. ET.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Best International Oscar race is the biggest ever — a record 104 international features are in contention, beating the previous high-water mark of 93 set in 2020 — and one of the most open in years.

There is no out-and-out favorite this season, although European cinema again looks strong, with Javier Calvo and Javier Abrosso’s Spanish entry La Bola Negra; Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’Or winner Fjord, in the running for Romania; and Pawel Pawlikowski’s Polish contender Fatherland all expected to make the short list, alongside Asian faves including South Korea’s Possible Love, from Lee Chang-dong; and Japan’s All of a Sudden from Ryusuke Hamaguchi.

Industry observers note that behind that top five is a long list of maybes, including French entry Minotaur from twice-nominated Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev; Lukas Dhont’s WWI drama Coward, Belgium’s entry; Austria’s Rose, which like Fatherland stars Sandra Huller; and Rehearsals for a Revolution, Pegah Ahangarani’s documentary on her family and their battles against the Iranian regime, which is the U.K. official Oscar submission.

Industry observers note that one hundred films were submitted by countries or regions. Four qualified through a new method where movies that win top awards at leading festivals are accepted as long as they meet the language, creative input and theatrical-release requirements for the category. According to Academy rules, an international feature film is defined as a feature-length motion picture (more than 40 minutes) produced outside the United States with a predominantly (more than 50 percent) non-English dialogue track. New Zealand’s submission, Taratoa Stappard’s gothic horror tale Mārama, was dropped for falling short of the language requirement.

Industry observers note that academy members from all branches who meet the minimum viewing requirements can participate in the preliminary round of voting for the shortlist, taking place between will take place Dec. 7-11. The shortlist of 15 international films will be revealed on Dec. 15. Oscar nominations voting will take place Jan. 11-15, 2027, with the nominations announcement on Jan. 21.

The 99th Academy Awards will be held on March 14, 2027.

THR has exhaustively compiled the full list of international contenders, with trailers, reviews and talent interviews where available. Enjoy!

It has been revealed that roland Sejko’s documentary uses archival footage, newsreels and state-produced cinema to examine how Enver Hoxha’s communist regime used film as an instrument of propaganda. Tracing Albania’s isolation and political transformation over four decades, the film explores how the country’s official image was manufactured, controlled and disseminated by the state.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

According to recent reports, in 1993, a car crash leaves Ahmed amnesiac, so that not even his family feels familiar. His youngest son fears him and his bandaged face, while Ahmed feels uneasy about his neighbor. Yanis Koussim’s debut feature — the Arabic title means “exorcism” — reimagines the traumas of Algeria’s bloody “Black Decade” (1992–2002), a civil war between the government and Islamist rebel groups, as a horror film, blending memory, trauma and possession.

Sources indicate that teenage angst meets the supernatural in Laura Casabé’s coming-of-age horror film, set over a single lazy summer day in 2001, at the peak of Argentina’s great depression. Amid the backdrop of social unrest, adolescent desire turns deadly in this slow-burn rage thriller, which debuted at Sundance in 2025.

Tamara Stepanyan’s narrative feature debut follows Céline, a French woman who travels to Armenia to settle the affairs of her supposedly deceased husband, Arto. There she discovers that he concealed his past as a soldier and is regarded by some as a deserter. As she investigates his life, Céline encounters a country still haunted by successive wars and their unresolved consequences.

Read THR‘s interview with director Tamara Stepanyan here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Industry observers note that james J. Robinson’s debut feature is the country’s first-ever Tagalog-language submission for the Oscars. The meditative film focuses on an aging woman who questions her faith as the world crumbles around her. After a young construction worker dies under suspicious circumstances, an elderly nun whose life has been shaped by discipline, service and belief, gets drawn into a world of crime and corruption.

The trailer for First Light is below.

Recent findings suggest that sandra Hüller is everywhere in this season’s awards conversation, but the German star gives her most transformative performance playing a 17th-Century woman passing as a male farmer in Markus Schleinzer’s period drama. Hüller won the Best Performance trophy in Berlin for the role, which was based on hundreds of similar recorded cases throughout history. Read THR’s review of Rose here.

In a recent development, zaur Gasimli’s historical drama follows Azerbaijani philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev and his efforts to establish Baku’s first school for Muslim girls in 1901. Facing fierce opposition from religious conservatives, Taghiyev enlists the support of his young wife, Sona, in a campaign that becomes a test of his influence, diplomacy and determination to expand educational opportunities for women.

Recent findings suggest that mejbaur Rahman Sumon reimagines Adam and Eve in the monsoon-soaked Bengali countryside in this dark folk tale. A tenant farmer (Mostafizur Noor Imran) wants out of his arranged marriage to a woman (Nazifa Tushi) the villagers regard as insane. Promising her a trip to the circus, he rows her into the forest and slips away in the dark. Yet however far he takes her, the thud of a palm fruit beside their hut confirms her return. Sumon’s follow-up to Hawa, Bangladesh’s 2022 Oscar submission, premiered in Rotterdam’s Tiger Competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

It has been revealed that lukas Dhont’s queer World War I drama follows two Belgian soldiers, Pierre and Francis, who find an unexpected refuge from the brutality of the trenches in the world of theatre. Assigned to organize entertainment for their fellow troops, the men develop an increasingly intimate relationship as they put together a revue behind the front lines. Leads Emmanuel Macchia and Valentin Campagne shared the Best Actor prize at Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

This Turkish-language political drama from German Academy Award nominee İlker Çatak (The Teacher’s Lounge) qualified for Oscar submission by winning the Golden Bear for Best Film at the Berlinale. Özgü Namal and Tansu Biçer star as Derya and Aziz, a successful theatrical couple whose lives are upended after their latest production brings them into conflict with the authorities in Ankara. Dismissed from their jobs and forced to leave their home, they find their loss of professional standing and financial security puts their marriage under pressure, testing the convictions that once united them.

Read THR‘s interview with Çatak here and THR‘s review of Yellow Letters here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

The coming-of-age drama about tradition, ambition and choosing your own destiny follows a young woman in the Bolivian Andes who takes up the sacred ways of midwifery, but dreams of escaping to the city to become a singer. Directed by Álvaro Olmos Torrico, The Condor Daughter had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival.

Sources indicate that A 60-something electrician has his very ordered life shattered by the sudden death of his wife. Left alone and forced to fend for himself in a strictly patriarchal society, he begins to recognize how much he took her devotion for granted. His attempts to reconnect with his estranged children are further complicated by his discovery that his son is living with another man.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Allan Deberton’s queer coming-of-age drama, which debuted in Berlin as part of the Generation Kplus section, follows a 12 year-old boy growing up in a small rural community trying balance his affection and desires with the fear of rejection from his father and surrounding community.

Check out a THR interview about the film here and the trailer below.

Nearly a decade after well-received 2017 feature Western, German director Valeska Grisebach returns with another deconstruction of a male-dominated genre. This slow-burning crime thriller, set in the Bulgarian borderlands, works as a low-key arthouse take on The Godfather, as archaeologist Veska (Yana Radeva) returns to the rural community she grew up in and reconnects with old friends, getting pulled back into criminal activity. Winner of the Jury Prize in Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Majid Majidi’s social drama, about Solan (Mohammad Rahimi), a poorly-paid temporary teacher in a remote, drought-stricken Iranian village was the stand out at this year’s Busan Film Festival, where it won the top prize, directly qualifying it for the Oscar race. When the death of the benefactor funding the school’s meal programme threatens to drive away the pupils, Solan takes matters into his own hands, turning to oil smuggling to keep the meals coming.

Check out the trailer for Midday Meal below.

It has been revealed that even the dead face eviction in Polen Ly’s elegiac ghost story about the cost of redevelopment in Cambodia. Thida (Savorn Serak) has watched over a movie house in Battambang since her death during the Khmer Rouge years. With the building marked for demolition, she must choose between wandering as a homeless spirit and risking the pain of another human life. She befriends Hai (Piseth Chhun), a young journalist who remembers going to the movies there as a boy. In the shuttered theater, the two watch a film together on his phone. Ly’s fiction feature debut premiered in Venice’s Biennale College Cinema program and won the Golden Hanoman, the top prize at Indonesia’s Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival.

According to recent reports, nchini Sylvia-Bright is back in her second Cameroon Oscar submission after Ngang Romanus’ 2021 movie Hidden Dreams. In Mabanda, she plays Mojoko, a pregnant teenager who, after the death of her mother, is left alone with her abusive father, played by director Quintus, and faces rejection by her community. Shot in Cameroonian Pidgin English, it’s the eighth submission by the country for the Academy Awards.

Check out the first look trailer below.

It has been revealed that this transatlantic drama from Montreal-based director Geneviève Dulude-De Celles bowed in Berlin, where it won the Silver Bear for Best Screenplay. It centers on an art expert, Mihail, who fled Bulgaria 30 years earlier and returns to authenticate the work of Nina, an 8-year-old Bulgarian artist and possible child prodigy, whose paintings have gone viral online. As Mikhail studies her work, he is forced to confront the ghosts of his past.

Check out the trailer for Nina Rosa below.

It has been revealed that the period mystery, the director’s second feature, premiered at Cannes. The follow-up to Martelli’s General Augusto Pinochet-era political thriller Chile ‘76is set in 1992, after Pinochet’s regime ends and a 9-year old girl is staying in an Andean ski resort where she befriends a German teenager aiming to be a competitive skier, only to vanish without a trace.

Read the THR review and an interview with Martelli.

Check out the trailer for The Meltdown below.

In a recent development, chinese comedy star Shen Teng plays a chef who takes a job in Bahata, a fictional stand-in for Baghdad, to pay off his family’s debts. In this war drama loosely inspired by the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, the Chinese restaurant where he works becomes both a refuge for local orphans and a bar for American soldiers. Director Wen Muye previously made a blockbuster out of the high cost of cancer drugs in China with 2018’s Dying to Survive. This latest social drama has grossed $358.4 million worldwide, making it by far the highest-grossing entry in this year’s international feature Oscar race.

A group of misfits converging at Babel, a legendary Colombian dive bar that doubles as purgatory, and where La Flaca — the city’s Grim Reaper — presides. Here, souls gamble years of their lives with her, daring to outwit Death herself. With his feature debut, which debuted at Sundance in 2025, director Gala del Sol has created a fantastical Colombian fever dream where life and death collides and the fate of people is left to chance.

Check out the official trailer below.

It has been revealed that with her debut feature, Costa Rica’s Kim Torres has created a rural chiller, combining story combining a coming-of-age drama with supernatural and thriller elements. The film follows 13-year-old Laura, who feels suffocated by her latest family, despite the lush forests and palm plantations that surround her. She soon discovers the supposed village paradise hides a shadowy secret that preys on the women living in it. Torres’ drama world premiered at San Sebastian’s New Directors sidebar in 2025.

Industry observers note that director Hana Jusic took inspiration from Wuthering Heights and gothic horror in this period drama, set in rural Croatia, circa 1910, to tell a surprisingly modern tale of female liberation. Teresa, a Chilean woman dressed all in black like an avenging angel, arrives in an isolated, and deeply religious community of Croatian shepherds in the early 20th century, claiming to be the widow of a local man who emigrated to South America.

Her arrival unsettles the tightly ordered society, challenging its traditional relationships and expectations. Unable to speak the language, she becomes a blank canvas for hopes and fears, particularly of the women in the community.

You can read a director interview here and watch the THR Presents interview with Hana Jusic here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Carlos Larrazabal’s debut feature explores the pull of home and the longing to leave. It follows Elvis, who returns to Havana after spending a decade in prison for murdering his abusive stepfather. As he reconnects with childhood sweetheart and falls back into life in the city’s criminal underworld, Elvis must decide whether to stay in the world he knows or escape Havana for a upcoming life elsewhere.

Industry observers note that cyprus’ first-ever international Oscar contender is also the feature debut of writer-director Myrsini Aristidou. Newcomer Maria Petrova and Christos Passalis, who played the son in Yorgos Lanthimos’ Dogtooth, star as an 11-year-old and her absent, petty criminal father who returns home after a family death. The film won The World Cinema Dramatic Audience Award at Sundance.

Check out the THR’s Presents interview with Myrsini Aristidou here and read an earlier interview with her here.

Sources indicate that prague-based filmmaker Pepa Lubojacki scoured through family photos and diary snapshots for this intimate, heart-rending look at her family’s struggles with alcoholism, addiction and homelessness. The film premiered in Berlin, where it won the best documentary honor as well as the independent Caligari award.

Industry observers note that this historical thriller from directors Yohane Dean Lengol and Hamed Mobasser is set in 1959, in the final months of Belgian colonial rule, in Club Rumba Royale, a popular nightclub where white Europeans and Congolese citizens rub shoulders as dance mixes with debates of independence. Featuring African rumba star Fally Ipupa, the feature is the first submission by DR Congo since 1997 and only the second overall.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

Sources indicate that may el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion-winning Woman Unknown is backdropped by a Danish city free from Nazi occupation, mere months after World War II has ended. It tells the story of Marie (Volpi Cup winner Mathilde Arcel), a young nanny and housemaid about to marry her wealthy, older, and widowed employer, Christian (Carsten Bjørnlund). But Marie guards a shameful secret.

Sources indicate that the Danish filmmaker deftly scrutinizes post-war patriotism and the era’s chastisement of women and their sex lives. “There have been so many films about the Second World War, and that is true,” el-Toukhy told THR ahead of Venice. “But they’re all based mostly on men’s experiences and recollections of war. So that really energized me.”.

Read THR‘s interview with May el-Toukhy here.

Check out a clip from Woman Unknown below.

The second feature film from director Andrés Farías centers on Sonia (Mercedes Morales), a widow who trades her family home for a cramped apartment and finds unexpected intimacy with Aimé, a working-class Haitian man, defying her family and the racial tensions between Dominicans and Haitians. The drama played Havana, Miami and Chicago and won best film, director and actress at the 2026 Dominican Film Festival in New York.

According to recent reports, director Cristina Barragán, who represented Ecuador in 2016 with Alba, continues her exploration of childhood wounds in this drama starring Simone Bucio as Azucena, a woman in her 30s who approaches Julio, a teenager in a group home, played by first-time actor Francis Eddú Llumiquinga. As they spend time together, an uneasy closeness grows, changing the personal bond in ways two outsiders from different worlds, but with a shared experience of trauma, The film won the best screenplay award in the Orizzonti section at the Venice Film Festival.

It has been revealed that the Egyptian-Austrian filmmaker Abu Bakr Shawky is back in the international Oscar race after his 2018 feature Yomeddine, also submitted for Egypt. The Stories, loosely inspired by his own parents’ relationship, follows aspiring Cairo pianist Ahmed and his long-distance romance with Austrian pen pal Liz, from the 1960s through the 1980s. Starring Amir El-Masry (The Crown) and Valerie Pachner (Fantastic Beasts: The Secrets of Dumbledore).

Read what the director said about The Stories here and then check out the trailer below.

Arturo López Rodas wrote, directed and produced this debut feature, a 60-minute drama in which three old friends reunite for a funeral after decades apart, musing on life, loss and time. It won best screenplay at the Ícaro Awards and best international feature at the Cobb International Film Festival. Vértices represents El Salvador’s first entry into Oscar’s best international feature competition.

Check out the official trailer below.

In his feature film debut, director German Golub charts the real-life story of Erika Salumäe, a track cyclist who overcomes personal and professional hardship — and the pressure of the dwindling Soviet regime — to become a two-time Olympic gold medallist in 1988 and 1992. From troubled young woman to national hero, Salumäe’s tenacity makes this biographical sports drama a story of inspiration and grit, with Estonian actress Karolin Jürise in the titular role.

Check out the trailer for Our Erika below.

Industry observers note that finnish filmmaker Markus Lehmusruusu (2019’s Ricky Rapper and the Strong Man) turns to science fiction in his sophomore feature. In a future, sterile world without nature or animals, Pasi (Miro Lopperi) is a lonely and compassionate designer of synthetic pets.

When by chance he stumbles upon the last surviving squirrel, he decides to defy the very strict regulations of interaction with what little nature is left in the world and help the squirrel back into its natural habitat. Lehmusruusu tackles the intersection of humanity’s instinctive need to both survive and provide in this Fantastic Fest debut (which used real, trained squirrels over animatronics or VFX).

Check out the trailer for The Squirrel below.

The first feature film from exiled Russian dissident director Andrey Zvyagintsev (Loveless, Leviathan) in nearly a decade is a taut psychological thriller set in Russia shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Loosely inspired by Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969) it follows a wealthy businessman caught between government demands that he recruit employees to send as cannon fodder in the war effort, and his growing suspicions that his wife is having an affair. As pressure mounts on both fronts, his carefully controlled domestic and professional life begins to unravel. Like the Russian state, he goes to extremes of violence to maintain the appearance of power and control.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Andrey Zvyagintsev here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Sources indicate that levan Koguashvili’s dramedy is set in a Georgian village struggling to recover from the economic upheaval following the collapse of the Soviet Union. At its center is Zuriko, a widowed hazelnut farmer trying to secure a fair price for his harvest while his debts mount. With the help of his friend Gela, he also embarks on a search for a new partner, despite the objections of his formidable former mother-in-law.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

Birgit Minichmayr plays Ella, a mother struggling to process the death of her daughter Jessie, in Sandra Wollner’s drama about grief and the complicated bonds left behind. Ella begins spending time with Lux, Jessie’s boyfriend, who was with her on the night she died. As the two grow closer, their relationship becomes increasingly entangled with memories of the young woman. An impulsive family holiday to Tenerife becomes an increasingly surreal attempt to escape grief and reconnect with the past.

A favorite in Cannes, where it won Best Film of the Un Certain Regard section, Everytime has been nominated for Best Film and Wollner for Best Screenplay at the 2027 European Film Awards.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Sandra Wollner here.

Check out the teaser for the film below.

Sources indicate that yannis Economides crafts a modern Greek tragedy out of the story of a businessman who devises what appears to be a foolproof scheme to save his family home from falling into the hands of a loan shark. But his plan sets a series of increasingly unpredictable events in motion, threatening to destroy the very life he is trying to preserve.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Guatemalan auteur Jayro Bustamante returns with an action-tinged drama inspired by the true story of Guatemala’s 2018 Volcán de Fuego tragedy. María Mercedes Coroy plays a volcanologist who tries to warn and evacuate Indigenous communities as a latest volcano forms amid corruption and economic interests. This is Bustamante’s fourth Oscar submission, after 2015’s Ixcanul, 2019’s La Llorona (shortlisted) and Rita from 2024.

Check out the official trailer (no subtitles) below.

Sources indicate that snow falls on Hong Kong in Juno Mak’s underworld epic, in which a hospital bombing kills a pharmaceutical magnate and leaves his younger son with an unusual ambition for a family drug empire — to shut it all down. A long-in-the-making saga starring Asian industry heavyweights Takeshi Kaneshiro, Tony Leung Ka-fai and Louis Koo, the film premiered in Cannes and won eight Hong Kong Film Awards, including one for its score by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto.

Industry observers note that tony Leung Chiu-wai, Léa Seydoux and fast-rising German star Luna Wedler feature in this century-spanning contemplative drama from Hungarian auteur Ildikó Enyedi (On Body and Soul, The Story of My Wife). Set in three different eras — 1908, 1972, and 2020 — it follows three very different people, a pioneering female student, a lovesick young man and a Hong Kong neuroscientist who share a connection to an ancient ginkgo tree growing int the botanical garden of a German university town. Enigmatic but never self-serious, Silent Friend leavens its big ideas and visual poetry with a healthy dose of deadpan humor.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with Silent Friend star Luna Wedler here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Industry observers note that yrsa Roca Fannberg turns her camera on the residents and caregivers of a Reykjavík nursing home in this observational documentary about ageing and the final stages of life. Everyday activities, from dancing and exercise classes to painting nails and sharing quiet moments, become the focus of an intimate portrait of a community negotiating the realities of old age. Rather than concentrating on decline, the film finds moments of companionship, humour and pleasure in the routines of institutional life.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Industry observers note that set in a remote Naga village near the Myanmar border in the early 1960s, Theja Rio’s debut feature follows Anghba, the community’s last surviving chief. With most of the villagers having left, he remains with his ailing wife and speech-impaired son, struggling to preserve the traditions of his ancestors. The arrival of an American missionary introduces Christianity and latest social customs, deepening the generational divide between father and son. The film won the Platform Award at Toronto, qualifying it for the Oscar race.

Read THR India‘s review of Angh here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Recent findings suggest that in Santosh Davakhar’s Marathi-language folk thriller, a young bride in rural Maharashtra plots her groom’s murder during the traditional ceremony meant to bless their marriage. As the village gathers for the gondhal, an all-night ritual of devotional song and dance, Suman (Ishita Deshmukh) recruits the groom’s cousin, a former suitor, to do the killing so she can run away with one of the performers. The film won Davakhar the Silver Peacock for best director at the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

Director Kamila Andini (Yuni) drew on the testimony of sexual assault survivors for this magical realist drama about the patriarchal structures of a Javanese mountain village. Putri Marino plays Pertiwi, who spent 20 years in prison for killing an accomplice to her rape at 16. She comes home to find the men who sent her away now running the village. When she meets a deaf teenage girl whose ordeal echoes her own, Pertiwi rallies her fellow outcasts to bring the abuse to light. The film premiered in Toronto, and Marino shared the best performance prize at the Singapore International Film Festival.

Babak Khajehpasha’s anti-war drama captures the lives and dreams of children and adults in Gaza against the backdrop of an ongoing conflict and crisis with Israel. The film cast child actors of Arab, Iranian, Syrian, and Lebanese backgrounds alongside Iranian performers.

Rather than depict violent battlefield scenes, the Iranian filmmaker focused on the all-too human impact of war on children as they learn fear, death and waiting are part of their everyday lives. The film also strikes a note of hope that love and life can be kept alive during horrific war and strife.

In a recent development, the Iraqi feature, which premiered out of competition in Venice, follows a female Kurdish sniper, Vyan, who returns to Mosul to try and rescue her younger sister. She has survived war by suppressing her emotions. When she learns that her younger sister, missing since the ISIS assault in 2014, may still be alive, she goes all out to rescue her. Mustafa, who was born in Iraqi Kurdistan and fled to Norway as a child, found inspiration for the film from an encounter with a female Peshmerga sniper during the 2014 frontline battles, as female Kurdish fighters countered Islamic State attacks.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

A robbery at a rural credit union ends in tragedy, but Damian McCann’s Irish-language thriller works backwards to reveal how three women became involved in the botched operation. Carrie Crowley, Bríd Brennan and Eva-Jane Gaffney star as the unlikely accomplices at the center of a story involving desperation, criminal ambition and a woman on the verge of a breakdown.

Check out the trailer for Aontas below.

According to recent reports, the Israeli film, set in 1987, centers on a 12-year-old boy, Boaz, who while preparing for his bar mitzvah is shocked to witness his father having sex in a swimming pool locker room. The boy’s family life is upturned just as the AIDS epidemic takes hold. But a decade later, the father and his older son attempt to reconcile and accept one another.

Rosenthal’s film, titled Independence in Hebrew, premiered at Sundance and won the top best picture award at Israel’s Ophir Awards, automatically making it the country’s Academy Awards entry.

Check out the trailer for Tell Me Everything below.

Paolo Strippoli’s psychological thriller is one of the rare genre romps among the mostly serious dramas in this season’s international Oscar race. Jasmine Trinca plays a housewife so desperate to have the perfect family she makes a faustian bargain with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi’s chain-smoking stranger, triggering a series of events that, over the course of decades, will bring her family crashing down. New Line has already snatched up English remake rights to this twisty crowd pleaser.

Read THR‘s review of The Spiral here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s first French feature begins as a workplace drama set in a nursing home outside Paris and blossoms into a love story about two women falling for each other’s minds. Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira) asks her overstretched nurses to employ a more humane system of care for residents living with dementia. Watching a play about life in a psychiatric institution, she recognizes her own convictions in the work of its Japanese director, Mari (Tao Okamoto), who is dying of cancer.

The women connect and talk deep into the night, slipping between French and Japanese, and there’s such pleasure in their exchanges that even Mari’s impromptu whiteboard lecture on capitalism feels like a moment of deep emotional connection. Efira and Okamoto shared the best actress prize at Cannes. After winning the international feature Oscar for Drive My Car in 2022, Hamaguchi is again considered a frontrunner this season.

Read THR‘s interview with All of a Sudden co-stars Tao Okamoto and Virginie Efira here.

The film’s official trailer is below.

According to recent reports, sink is a drama about a mother navigating her son’s mental health crisis — still a taboo subject in Jordan — by denying her son’s struggles and opting instead to see his emotional withdrawal and disruptive behavior at school as teenage rebellion. So the mother follows her son about with devotion, hoping her guidance at attention will prove a cure. Duraie’s debut feature, following her acclaimed short films Horizon and Give up the Ghost, had its world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival, nd.

It has been revealed that abel is a shepherd living on a collective farm in Kazakhstan whose life in thrown into turmoil in the 1990s when, following the collapse of the Soviet Union, collective farms were dismantled and divided up among corrupt leaders. The aging Abel has a choice: play along for a piece of the action or stand up for what he believes is right.

Check out the trailer below (no English subtitles).

According to recent reports, writer-director Vincho Nchogu serves up a mix of comedy and drama in her feature debut. Sarah Karei plays Star, an orphaned and unmarried 38-year-old woman in a rural village who risks losing her home unless she can prove her family lineage and claim her land deed. Along the way she has to deal with hostile neighbors, shady organizations and the promise of potential romance. Winner of the audience award at Tribeca and the Best First Feature prize at the BFI London Film Festival.

Blerta Basholli takes a coming-of-age story into the increasingly volatile atmosphere of late-1990s Kosovo. Thirteen-year-old Dua is navigating the usual uncertainties of adolescence when an incident turns her into a target within her community. Her friendship with the outspoken Maki offers a fresh perspective on the world around her, even as the escalating conflict threatens to overwhelm their lives.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Bekzat Pirmatov blends psychological horror, folklore and family drama in this supernatural tale about a grieving woman plagued by a recurring nightmare in which an unseen presence appears to strangle her in her sleep. Seeking an explanation, she turns to a traditional healer who discovers ominous markings on the bodies of pregnant women. Their investigation leads to the ancient Kyrgyz legend of Albarsty, a malevolent female spirit associated with pregnancy and childbirth.

A biographical sports drama from Viesturs Kairišs, who co-wrote Ulya with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, Livia Ulman, and Andris Feldmanis. The Cannes-premiering, black-and-white feature is set in rural Soviet Latvia in 1964, where Uļjana “Ulya” Semjonova’s (Kārlis Arnolds Avots) attracts the attention of basketball scouts due to her exceptional height and strength. She’s pulled from farm life into elite sport in this mise-en-scène-embracing portrait of a Latvian legend.

Read THR‘s interview with director Viesturs Kairišs here.

Check out THR‘s portrait of Ulya star and co-screenwriter Karlis Arnolds Avots here.

It has been revealed that lebanon’s Oscar hopeful is a heist thriller about two sisters who concoct an elaborate initiative to break into a bank to steal their own money — the cash frozen by the government during the 2019 Lebanese liquidity crisis — to fund a life-saving operation. Director Rami Kodeih co-wrote the film with his wife Nora Mariana inspired by their own experience at the time, when Mariana needed surgery and their savings were inaccessible. George Clooney and Grant Heslov are executive producers for Smokehouse Pictures.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Check out a clip from the film below.

Recent findings suggest that how to Divorce During the War is exactly as it sounds — a high-flying executive Marija (Zygimante Elena Jakstaite) chooses the worst possible moment to inform her struggling filmmaker husband Vytas (Marius Repsys) she wants to split up: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Vilnius-set, soul-searching drama won director Andrius Blaževičius a directing award upon its Sundance premiere.

This jump scare-heavy psychological horror from debut feature filmmaker Cyrus Neshvad (already an Oscar nominee for 2023 short The Red Suitcase) follows a family in dire straits. With their young son not having much time left, Anne and Greg are ready to sacrifice everything to give him one last chance at salvation. But after crossing an unforgivable moral line, they find themselves trapped in a nightmare where every choice comes with an ever-higher price. Child earned its world premiere at the 2026 Raindance Film Festival.

Check out the official trailer below.

Woo Ming Jin drew on his own childhood as a twin for this coming-of-age drama about two teenage brothers in a Malaysian coastal town. At 15, Ali is the only person who understands his twin brother Amir’s way of communicating. When their father remarries, he packs the boys off to work in a salted-fish factory. But it’s their shared crush on their upcoming English teacher (Indonesian star Dian Sastrowardoyo) that turns the brothers into rivals. The film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival.

Żejtune is a visually rich Maltese-language drama from the New York-based Alex Camilleri, led by Michela Farrugia as Mar. When her estranged mother passes away, Mar sees her way out of Malta by selling off her inheritance: three pieces of farmland in the countryside. On her journey to claim her land, she meets Nenu, a spirited 80-year-old singer (Nenu Borg) whose vibrant folk music pulls her into the colourful traditions of the island she’s been so eager to escape. The movie hit the festival circuit with appearances at Gothenburg and Tribeca.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

According to recent reports, david Pablos’ drama follows Veneno (Víctor Prieto), a rebellious young drifter who sleeps with truckers at roadside diners. He persuades one of his hook ups, Muñeco (Osvaldo Sánchez) to take him deep into the hyper-masculine world of long-haul trucking. The road movie, produced by Diego Luna, won best film in Venice’s Orizzonti section as well as the Queer Lion.

Read THR‘s review of On The Road here.

Mongolia’s struggle to end more than two centuries of Qing rule takes the shape of an espionage thriller in Tamir Bat-Ulzii’s sweeping historical epic. The actor-director casts himself as Namnansuren, the statesman who joined forces with the Buddhist leader Bogd Khan in 1911. The conspirators seek help from Russia while building a network of spies at home. Made to mark the 115th anniversary of Mongolia’s declaration of independence, the film became one of the country’s biggest local hits this year.

Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić drummed up excitement in Sundance with To Hold a Mountain, a documentary shot in the Montenegrin highlands where a shepherdess and her adopted daughter are haunted by the violent death of her mother and must defend their mountain against its transformation into a NATO military training ground. This tender, windswept feature picked up the Grand Jury Prize in Sundance and the Heart of Sarajevo in the fest’s documentary competition section.

Recent findings suggest that laïla Marrakchi offers a upcoming spin on the familiarly-bleak tale of migrant labor and exploitation in this social realist drama, inspired by real-life cases of Moroccan women who travel to Spain to work as seasonal fruit-pickers. Her protagonist Hasna (Nisrin Erradi) is a flawed, even unlikable character doing what she needs to survive in a world where oppression and coercion are the norm. Strawberries premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section.

Read THR‘s interview with Laila Marrakchi here.

Recent findings suggest that abinash Bikram Shah’s debut, the first Nepali feature to screen in Cannes’ Official Selection, won the jury prize in Un Certain Regard. The richly-realized missing-person thriller follows Pirati (Pushpa Thing Lama), the matriarch of a Kinnar community of trans women in rural Nepal. Pirati dreams of slipping away with the man she loves. But when one of the young women she calls her daughters vanishes on a night patrol to keep wild elephants out of the village, she puts those plans on hold to search for her.

Read THR India’s interview with Abinash Bikram Shah here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Sources indicate that afghan-Dutch filmmaker Dawood Hilmandi turns the camera on his own family history in this intimate documentary about war, exile and an attempt at reconciliation with his estranged father. Having fled Afghanistan and later Iran, Hilmandi has made a home in Amsterdam, but a personal loss prompts him to return to his father, an aging, authoritarian former mujahideen fighter. Together they revisit the past, travelling between Iran and Afghanistan in an effort to overcome decades of silence, inherited trauma and estrangement. The film won three prizes at IDFA, including Best First Feature and the FIPRESCI international critics award.

Check out the trailer for Paikar below.

Sisters Ade and Titi lead very different lives under the shadow of their late father. The older Ade (Bimbo Akintola) is a devout Christian and the family’s sole breadwinner, while Titi (Tosin Adeyemi) is an aspiring singer full of independent spirit. When their ailing mother comes to live with them, old resentments resurface, forcing both sisters to confront grief and the fragile bonds that hold a family together.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

Kosara Mitić’s debut feature 17, co-written by Ognjen Sviličić, arrived at this year’s Berlinale with a fierce exploration of sexual trauma and female solidarity. The movie follows seventeen-year-old Sara (Eva Kostic), who’s hiding a secret during a school trip. When the trip spirals out of control and she witnesses her friend Lina being sexually assaulted, the two girls try to break the cycle of casual violence and seal an everlasting bond between them in the process.

Read THR‘s interview with 17 director Kosara Mitić here.

Sources indicate that hans Petter Moland adapts Knut Hamsun’s Nobel Prize-winning novel about a man determined to make a life in the Norwegian wilderness. Isak arrives in the remote landscape with little more than his willingness to work the land. His relationship with Inger leads to a family and a more permanent settlement, but the couple’s struggle to survive the harsh conditions is gradually complicated by the arrival of the outside world.

Check out the trailer for The Growth of the Soil below.

In August 2023, eight passengers, six of them schoolboys, found themselves dangling in a cable car 900 feet above a ravine in northern Pakistan. Mohammed Ali Naqvi pieced together what followed from cellphone and drone footage, interviews and re-creations, as army commandos and local volunteers raced to save them. The film premiered at Sundance and is the first documentary Pakistan has submitted for the international feature Oscar.

Read THR’s review of Hanging by a Wire here.

Read THR‘s interview with Mohammed Ali Naqvi here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Osama is a professional photographer, and newly introduced father, living in Gaza who, at the start of the Gaza war, turns to photojournalism to support his wife and infant child. Balancing duty and hope, Ahmed Hassouna’s documentary provides a cinematic portrait of resilience and humanity in wartime. The last two Oscar submission from Palestine: Palestine 36 and From Ground Zero, both made the shortlist but were not nominated.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

The drama, from directors Aarón Bromley and Arturo Montenegro, is set in 1980s against backdrop of Peru’s war between the Shining Path guerrillas and the army. It follows Josué (Junior Bejar), who flees armed conflict in his Peruvian Andes village to migrate to Panama in pursuit of a boxing career and a better future.

Check out the trailer for Chichero below (no subtitles).

In a recent development, narciso, a charismatic musician with rock ’n’ roll in his veins, returns to Asunción from Buenos Aires and becomes a symbol of freedom after being found dead at the height of his career. This period drama is freely inspired by the 1959 killing of radio host Bernardo Aranda, which led the Paraguay dictatorship to persecute gay men. Written, produced, directed and edited by Marcelo Martinessi, whose The Heiresses was Paraguay’s 2018 Oscar submission, Narciso won the FIPRESCI Prize for best film in Berlin’s Panorama section.

Check out THR Espanol‘s review of Narciso here.

The film’s official trailer (without subtitles) is below.

According to recent reports, paolo Tizón’s visceral observational doc, which premiered at Karlovy Vary, chronicles young military recruits as they as they go through gruelling training in an elite Peruvian military unit battling drug trafficking. The filmmaker spent 10 months embedded with the recruits to capture the hermetic world in his directorial debut.

Check out the trailer for Night Has Come below.

Rafael Manuel turns a sweltering day at an exclusive golf club outside Manila into a deadpan, formalist satire of the Philippine class system. As 17-year-old Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) tees up balls for the wealthy members, Manuel often frames her face between a golfer’s legs. When she ventures beyond the driving range, even sneaking a taste of a cake the guests have left untouched feels like an act of defiance. Manuel expanded his Berlin Silver Bear-winning short into this debut feature, which won a special jury award for creative vision at Sundance.

Read THR‘s interview with Rafael Manuel here.

In a recent development, paweł Pawlikowski, an Oscar winner for Ida (2013) and Best Director and Best International Feature nominee for Cold War (2018), returns to European history with this black-and-white drama about German writer Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his journey back to his homeland in 1949 after 16 years in exile. Accompanied by his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) Mann travels across the country, now divided into a U.S.-supported West and a Soviet-controlled East, confronting the political and personal contradictions of postwar Germany, as well as his own complicated relationship with his homeland.

Read THR‘s review of Fatherland here.

Listen to THR‘s Awards Chatter interview with Fatherland star Sandra Hüller here.

Check out the trailer for the film below.

At 80, Arménio is finding it increasingly difficult to live independently and is reluctantly moved into a nursing home. A former soldier who fought in Portugal’s colonial war in Angola, he carries memories and prejudices that have never been fully confronted. António Ferreira’s drama follows his uneasy adjustment to institutional life and his developing friendship with Hermínia, a Black caregiver whose patience and compassion challenge his assumptions about the world and his own past.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Sources indicate that A Romanian couple’s attempt to build a newly introduced life in Norway becomes the subject of a bitter cultural and ideological confrontation in Cristian Mungiu’s latest drama. Lisbet and Mihai, played by Renate Reinsve and Sebastian Stan, are evangelical Christians whose approach to raising their children attracts the attention of local child-protection authorities. As allegations of abuse threaten to separate the family, the couple find themselves caught between their religious convictions and a state determined to intervene. Mungiu won his second Palme d’Or in Cannes this year with Fjord, and the film is an Oscar frontrunner.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR‘s interview with Fjord director Cristian Mungiu here.

Check out the trailer for Fjord below.

It has been revealed that this is a double debut – director Marie Clémentine Dusabejambo’s first feature and Rwanda’s inaugural international Oscar entry. The drama, which explores the long road to justice and reconciliation for survivors of the Rwandan genocide won both the Caméra d’Or for best first feature and the FIPRESCI international critics Prize at Cannes.

Read THR‘s review of the film here.

Read THR’s interview with Marie Clémentine Dusabejambo here.

Check out a teaser for the film below.

Sources indicate that anas Ba-Tahaf’s black comedy follows the complicated romance between a woman (Sarah Taibah, who also wrote the screenplay), convinced a generational curse will kill her on her 30th birthday, and a heart surgeon who, every operation, has to suppress his urge to kill his patients. Set in contemporary Jeddah, the film premiered at the Red Sea Film Festival last year.

Check out the trailer for ther film below.

This deeply personal documentary from director Mamadou Khouma Gueye (the title, Liti Liti, translates as “The Attachment”), is in the Guinaw-Rails neighborhood in the Senegalese capital of Dakar where the filmmaker grew up. The district is being bulldozed to make way for the Dakar Regional Express Train, leaving residents, such as the director’s mother, displaced. Senegal has only ever submitted six films for the Oscars, but three of them have made the shortlist.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Nenad Pavlović directs a screenplay from Jovan Popović in the arthouse indie Wanderlust. The black-and-white, self-described avant-garde film is based on the 1957 novel Izlet by Serbian painter and film director Mica Popovic. It follows a grieving young artist who flees society to create art in absolute solitude on a deserted island, only to learn that isolation can be as imprisoning as the world he left behind.

Koh Jia Ler was a schoolboy when Anthony Chen cast him opposite Yeo Yann Yann in Ilo Ilo, Singapore’s 2013 Oscar submission. In the final film of the trilogy Chen continued with Wet Season (2019), Koh plays a young man whose girlfriend is pregnant. His widowed father, a noodle seller, has fallen for a beer waitress played by Yeo. Chen’s portrait of two generations trying to build a family became the first Singaporean film selected for the Berlin International Film Festival’s main competition, where it received strong reviews.

THR‘s review of We Are All Strangers.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Production firm Silverart describes Martin Gonda’s feature debut as the highest-rated Slovak film of 2025. Inspired by true events — the displacement of the Rusyn people over the construction of the Starina reservoir — it is set in 1980 communist Czechoslovakia, where Mara (Sára Chripáková) dreams of leaving her village to study and become a pilot. But her father, a Rusyn farmer and widower, insists she stays and works the land. As the construction of the reservoir looms, Gonda depicts the struggle between tradition, identity, and the desire for freedom.

Check out the official trailer below.

It has been revealed that earning its world premiere at Locarno, Fantasy is from the mononymous Slovenian-Macedonian filmmaker Kukla (full name Katarina Rešek) in her feature film debut. Gender, desire and self-discovery come to the forefront in this tale of three best friends living in a fictional Slovenian industrial town. A chance encounter with Fantasy (Alina Juhart), a young transgender woman, might just change their lives for the better.

Read THR‘s interview with director Kukla here.

Check out the official trailer below.

Winner of the Tiger Award at this year’s Rotterdam Film Festival, this drama from co-directors Devon Delmar and Jason Jacobs tells the story of an 80-year-old Namaqualand goat herder who is in danger of losing her independence after she falls victim to a scam promising reparation for her father’s unpaid service during World War II. Jacobs cast his own grandmother to play the lead.

Read THR‘s interview with Delmar here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Eight years after Burning became the first South Korean film shortlisted for the international feature Oscar, Korean maestro Lee Chang-dong returned to Venice with a characteristically searing drama about what capitalism is doing to human dignity — and whether art has any power to critique the system that bankrolls it. Sul Kyung-gu plays an autoworker shattered by the violent end to a strike at his factory. His wife (Jeon Do-yeon) befriends a documentary filmmaker (Cho Yeo-jeong) whose tycoon husband (Zo In-sung) patiently supports her interest in workers’ rights.

According to recent reports, both a powerful love story and a meta-fictional exploration of the ethics of filmmaking, much of the film’s drama explores the slippery line between the artist’s sympathy for her subjects and the desire for a good scene. The Netflix film won Venice’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. Jeon, who previously became the first Korean to win best actress at Cannes for Lee’s Secret Sunshine, is now considered a strong contender in the lead actress Oscar race.

Read THR‘s review of Possible Love.

Read THR‘s interview with Lee Chang-dong.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

The sweeping gay historical epic La Bola Negra won Los Javis the coveted Best Director prize in Cannes this year, immediately entering the international — and domestic — awards conversation. Weaving together three interconnected storylines from 1932, 1937, and 2017, the critic darling puts queer desire, repression and Spain’s inherited stories up on the major screen, hurling breakout stars Guitarricadelafuente and Miguel Bernardeau into the mainstream and potentially giving The Odyssey a run for its Best Picture money.

Read THR‘s behind-the-scenes deep dive into the making of the film here.

Check out THR‘s portrait of La Bola Negra breakout star Guitarricadelafuente here.

Three police officers escort a prisoner across Sri Lanka’s Knuckles mountains toward the village where he grew up. The officers have reason to expect he won’t make it home alive. But it’s a long drive, and their captive proves an unexpectedly agreeable traveling companion. Lalith Rathnayake’s second feature won prizes for screenplay and cinematography in the Asian New Talent competition at the Shanghai International Film Festival.Official trailer below.

An ordinary family is crushed by economic forces beyond their control in director Visar Morina’s social drama, which won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize in Sundance, qualifying it for Oscar consideration. Husband and wife Hatixhe and Shaban work a small dairy farm in rural Kosovo to support their three daughters and extended family. But when a family dispute costs them their livelihood, they are forced to move to the capital Pristina in search of work, only to find themselves struggling with low wages and the high cost of housing.

Read THR‘s review of Shame and Money here.

Read THR‘s interview with director Visar Morina here.

In a recent development, podcaster and journalist Alex Schulman makes his feature film debut with Adult Supervision, a black comedy that allowed him to work with his once-public enemy Gustav Skarsgård. The second-born son of the Swedish family dynasty stars as anxiety-ridden Bill, who accompanies his daughter and her school friends on a remote trip, desperate to repair their icy relationship. He has help from two fellow fathers: the secretly domineering Bobo (Fares Fares) and Pontus (Linus Wahlgren), but tensions quickly escalate, and their grip on the situation begins to slip.

Read THR‘s interview with Alex Schulman here.

Check out the official trailer below.

Nicolas Wadimoff has long dominated the doc and feature film space with his politically provocative work, and continues that trend with the harrowing, Venice-premiering documentary Who Is Still Alive. Described by the filmmaker as “an absolute necessity,” the project spotlights nine voices from Gaza. The group — made up of women and men, old and young — reflects on life before and during the ongoing war with Israel, outlining their neighborhoods in chalk from memory and detailing their close relationships with the friends, neighbors and family they’ve now lost.

Read THR’s interview with Nicolas Wadimoff here.

Check out the film’s trailer below.

Shortly after Bashar al-Assad fell in December 2024, filmmaker Tawfik Sabouni returned to Saidnaya, the prison outside Damascus known as “the other side of the sun.” A former inmate, Sabouni invited four fellow survivors back into the cells to reconstruct for his camera the brutal rituals by which they had lived. The documentary premiered in Berlin’s Panorama section and won both the critics’ and audience prizes at the Amman International Film Festival.

Check out the trailer for The Other Side of the Sun below.

Industry observers note that in 1954, during Taiwan’s White Terror, a teenager travels alone from Chiayi to Taipei to buy back the body of her executed brother. She nearly falls into the hands of traffickers before a discharged soldier takes up her cause. Written and directed by Chen Yu-hsun (My Missing Valentine), the film won four Golden Horse Awards, including best narrative feature and original screenplay.

Check out the trailer for A Foggy Tale below.

Sompot Chidgasornpongse drew on the Buddhist pilgrimages of his childhood for this gently comic family road movie. When a fortune teller warns that his elderly mother may soon die, Sakol packs three generations into a van to visit nine temples in a single day. Nine is an auspicious number in Thailand, and Sakol hopes the family’s offerings to the monks will earn enough merit to prolong his mother’s life. A few stops in, Mom is too tired to get out of the van.

Produced by Chidgasornpongse’s longtime collaborator Apichatpong Weerasethakul, his fiction feature debut premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight and won directing and acting prizes in Shanghai’s Asian Upcoming Talent competition.

Check out the trailer to 9 Temples to Heaven below.

A retired civil engineer gives his Syrian caregiver money to take her two young sons to Europe. Instead, she leaves the boys with him and disappears, just as his grown children arrive for Eid al-Adha with claims of their own on the family’s resources. Tunç Davut’s family drama premiered at Turkey’s Antalya Film Festival.

Check out the trailer for Like a Limbless Tree below.

It has been revealed that trauma, resistance and hope loom large over Alisa Kovalenko’s Traces, which picked up the Berlinale’s audience award this year. The documentary follows the stories of six Ukrainian women — from Donbas to the Kherson region and the Kyiv area — who survived conflict-related sexual violence and torture during Russia’s aggression and refuse to remain silent.

The film’s official trailer is below.

Recent findings suggest that former child star and documentarian Pegah Ahangarani charts over 40 years of turbulent political history in Iran with Rehearsals for a Revolution, crafted entirely around her own family archives. The final product, which won Ahangarani Cannes’ Golden Eye award for best documentary, is a portrait of a country shaped by political repression and in constant hope for radical change.

It has been revealed that “I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,’” Ahangarani told THR about drawing inspiration from her relatives’ photos, videos and voice recordings. “Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship [and] the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe.”.

#140381. Industry News: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

Industry News: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen.
  • Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility.
  • Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.

Sources indicate that now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times.".

It has been revealed that atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Recent findings suggest that modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times.

In a recent development, the researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

Sources indicate that "It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a new technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.".

Sources indicate that that improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A Upcoming Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity.

It has been revealed that the findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening fresh possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

For now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the substantial next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.".

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

#140377. Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations.
  • According to recent reports, the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy.
  • Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

According to recent reports, the study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

It has been revealed that "This idea that relativity is crucial in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," said Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

In a recent development, some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

Industry observers note that the sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

For lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

In a recent development, heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become vital, changing how the electrons behave.

According to recent reports, one particularly important effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

According to recent reports, "The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang stated. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

To test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

The researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

By measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

In a recent development, rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

The findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the newly introduced textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang mentioned.

  • Recent findings suggest that in 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law.
  • After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”.

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put latest restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

In a recent development, but Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about prepares to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

Sources indicate that the CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

Sources indicate that so is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the challenges that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

It has been revealed that they’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

It sounds like CEOs are frustrated?

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

Sources indicate that you would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from significant business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

In a recent development, tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

It has been revealed that the first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two latest factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla mentioned there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

“Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”.
