📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki, two of Indian cinema’s most celebrated playback singers, were remembered at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa by singer K.S. Chithra and actor-filmmaker Suhasini Maniratnam.

Bhosle, a two-time Grammy nominee whose name was referenced in Cornershop’s 1997 hit “Brimful of Asha,” died in April at 92. Janaki, known as the Nightingale of South India, died in July at 88. Chithra and Suhasini shared their memories of the two at the annual “Lata Mangeshkar Talk: The Voice That Echoes Forever,” named for Bhosle’s elder sister, the singer Lata Mangeshkar. Related Stories Seth Rogen on ‘The Invite,’ ‘Tangles,’ ‘The Studio’ Season 2, Reviving ‘Darkwing Duck’ and Why ‘Any A--hole Can Write That Joke’ Was the Best Advice He Ever Got Oscar Predictions: Film Editing — ‘You Can See Everything’ Looks to Crash a Race of Past Winners and Become the Third Documentary Ever Nominated.

Chithra, who has recorded more than 25,000 songs in several Indian languages over a career spanning nearly five decades, spoke about the singers who shaped her musical sensibilities, among them Mangeshkar, P. Susheela and Janaki. She imitated Janaki as a child, while acknowledging that the veteran singer’s distinctive style was impossible to reproduce. Mangeshkar’s devotional songs, she said, had particularly impressed her with their emotional depth.

In a recent development, suhasini recalled an episode from the making of “Iruvar” (1997), directed by her husband Mani Ratnam. Composer A.R. Rahman, an Oscar winner for “Slumdog Millionaire,” had invited Bhosle to record a song that needed to evoke the style of Tamil playback singer L.R. Eswari, but was unsure how to explain the reference to her. He asked Suhasini to help. She demonstrated Eswari’s style, and Bhosle went on to deliver “Venilla Venilla.”.

Chithra spoke about Bhosle’s versatility and her ability to move between musical forms, including ghazals, and about her desire to establish her own musical identity rather than be compared with her sister. At their first meeting, Chithra said, Bhosle asked her why she was singing in such a high register.

Janaki, Suhasini remarked, could inhabit a character through her voice, singing like a child or a teenage boy. Chithra recalled that Janaki was a devoted fan of Mangeshkar. She would play Mangeshkar’s songs on the radio, turn down the volume during the vocal portions and record herself singing along – “like a karaoke on her own,” as Chithra described it. Offstage, Chithra said, Janaki would feed her by hand when she visited her home.

The session also touched on the demands of recording and on recognizing one’s vocal limitations with age.

According to recent reports, chithra sang snippets throughout, including songs from her own repertoire and numbers popularized by Janaki and Bhosle. In a closing quiz, film clips were played without their background scores and Chithra was asked to identify each song by singing it. She identified all five.

The session ended with Chithra singing “Paadariyen” from “Sindhu Bhairavi” (1985), which won her the first of her six National Film Awards, as Suhasini, who starred in the film, joined her, lip-syncing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that at first glance, everything seems to be business as usual.
  • "As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.
  • "If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that at first glance, everything seems to be business as usual. Lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, are holding four days of final debates on how much money the federal government may spend in the coming year, and on what. These follow a familiar pattern: The government pats itself on the back, while the opposition voices criticism. But anyone listening more closely will notice that there are doubts even in the ranks of the coalition parties, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), their Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

"As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.

"If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This government has now been in office for about 20 months. Back in early 2025, expectations were enormous. Merz had promised to bring the budget back in line with the debt brake enshrined in the constitution, which stipulates that the government can spend only slightly more than it collects (with exceptions now made for defense and security).

Yet for 2027, spending — at just under €561 billion ($614 billion) — will be higher than ever before, and tax revenues are nowhere near sufficient to cover this, meaning Germany is looking at record borrowing for the year totaling €210 billion.

Recent findings suggest that the largest opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) calculated that the government will incur €401,000 in latest debt every minute next year. In the Bundestag, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called it a "debt orgy" that will paralyze the country. Merz will "go down in history as the chancellor who led Germany to bankruptcy," he exclaimed.

Germany's budget deficit has only ever been higher in the COVID-19 pandemic. The current pressures are obvious: The economy is struggling, the population aging, and Russia's war against Ukraine is about to enter its sixth year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The defense budget is now by far the highest in the history of the Federal Republic, with €109 billion allocated for 2027, an increase of €27 billion on last year. Added to this is the multi-year, debt-financed special military fund, intended to modernize the armed forces, bringing the total defense budget to €139 billion.

The AfD and the socialist Left Party have sharply criticized this. Left Party parliamentary leader Heidi Reichinnek accused the government of pursuing "militarization and boundless rearmament on the one hand, and brutal social cuts and an orgy of budget cuts on the other.".

The AfD's Chrupalla remarked that the temporary reduction in the electricity tax, pushed through at the last minute, would save the average family a mere €100 a year, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "walks out of the chancellery here in Berlin with a check for €200 million after just one afternoon.".

"Whose chancellor are you, Mr. Merz?" he asked.

The opposition Greens did not agree. While they also criticized the budget as "unserious," Green Party Bundestag member Britta Haßelmann described the AfD's stance on Ukraine as shameful. She rejected the idea that money was being wasted on Ukraine, saying that supporting Ukraine bolstered security for Germany and Europe.

The chancellor shares this view. "You can't say it often enough, either to the far right or the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than just Ukraine," Merz said.

He added that Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and in space; and that Moscow is also seeking escalation in Germany, even at the cost of lives. "That is why we must show Russia its limits," he said.

In a recent development, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for the government to justify the high spending on Ukraine. Germany's pension and health care costs are only getting bigger: By far the largest single budget item is that of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is rising to over €200 billion, even with cuts to unemployment benefits.

Industry observers note that work is right now underway on a reform of the pension system — something that many see as urgent, as the workforce born in the 1960s, when more than a million children were born in Germany every year, is on brink of retiring. Birth rates nearly halved by the mid-1970s and declined even further afterward. For now, so-called "boomers" still make up one-third of the current workforce — but soon they will be drawing pensions.

It has been revealed that even now, Germany's pensions cannot be financed solely with contributions on wages and salaries. In 2025, just over €420 billion in pensions were paid out, with the government contributing €127 billion of that amount. By 2027, the government aims to save €3 billion on this figure, which is likely to further increase pension contributions.

Sources indicate that the coalition parties are stuck in a row over how to reform the pension system. Chancellor Merz insisted in the Bundestag that the coalition was solving the country's fundamental problems, but he warned that in future, tax revenues "will no longer be enough to afford everything we have become all too accustomed to," he remarked. "All of us here will have to give up some of the ideas we cherish.".

In a recent development, the SPD, on the other hand, is counting on increasing federal revenue. Its parliamentary leader Matthias Miersch emphasized in the Bundestag that large fortunes and inheritances must contribute more to "public costs.".

That, he noted, must also apply to large companies. Currently, heirs to family-owned businesses often pay significantly less in taxes than heirs to real estate or financial assets, because they can be exempted from inheritance tax if they continue to run the business. This is intended to protect them from having to pay taxes in the event of a breakup or sale of the organization.

Sources indicate that according to Miersch, the government must now think about taxing the wealthy more. "For us, this problem is by no means off the table; on the contrary, we are putting it on the agenda," he said. The government's revenue situation is "an issue we need to discuss.".

Sources indicate that all in all, the outlook for 2027 is strained — and not just financially. The political differences between the CDU/CSU and the SPD are likely to make working together even more difficult. Conflict is inevitable, especially with several state elections scheduled for the spring.

Recent findings suggest that the chancellor knows this and tried to appear confident that better collaboration was possible. "We must seek compromise in our joint decision-making, represented by these — admittedly quite different — coalition partners," he said.

This article was originally written in German.

#140344. Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing latest details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System.
  • New research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed.
  • Industry observers note that the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing latest details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide important clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

New research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

Industry observers note that the Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Crucial Clues.

Dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

"The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan mentioned.

In a recent development, "Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth.".

According to recent reports, "By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment.".

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts.

According to recent reports, to investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

In a recent development, these findings offer a new perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

In a recent development, the implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth.

In a recent development, "The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan noted.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a latest era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side.".

Sources indicate that the return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.
  • At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on complications ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.
  • In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a initiative to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on complications ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a initiative to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank.

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”.

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

Recent findings suggest that “Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”.

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”.

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn stated a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

According to recent reports, investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”.

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who noted he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out intends for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”.

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”.

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

In a recent development, the insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how swiftly the deal came together.

Industry observers note that “Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” remarked Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech.

Sources indicate that quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he stated he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

Director Francis Lawrence’s adaptation of author Suzanne Collins’ 2025 prequel novel is looking at a five-day sum around $85 million to take its domestic cume to roughly $233 million through Sunday. After opening to the fifth-biggest launch in Lionsgate history last weekend with $119 million domestically and $225 million worldwide, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping has continued its momentum. The $150 million-budgeted film, which earned an A- CinemaScore, grossed $15.98 million domestically on Tuesday to notch the franchise’s biggest first Tuesday, narrowly topping the $15.96 million for 2013’s Catching Fire. Sunrise’s Monday sum of $12.8 million also bested the series’ previous top opening Monday of $12.3 million for Catching Fire.

The East Coast has been impacted by a major storm stretching from the Midwest to the Eastern seaboard, leading the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Upcoming York to be moved to Saturday for the first postponement in its 100-year history. The inclement weather could slow down moviegoing throughout the weekend, including on Black Friday, which tends to be the biggest day for the box office over the Thanksgiving frame.

According to recent reports, disney released Hexed in 3,725 North American theaters on Wednesday, with the animated fantasy film collecting an estimated $7.6 million on opening day, including $2.1 million in Tuesday previews. Directors Jason Hand and Fawn Veerasunthorn’s movie, which carries a budget north of $200 million, could be heading for a five-day launch around $35 million. This looks to be down a bit from the $45 million opening that the studio had initially been projecting.

Sources indicate that hailee Steinfeld, Rashida Jones and Jodie Foster lead the voice cast for Hexed, which centers on a mother and her teenage daughter grappling with the girl’s magical powers. The studio has been hopeful that it will continue to run throughout the holiday corridor and follow the lead of this year’s original animated features with pleasing performances, including Goat and Hoppers, although other recent originals like Forgotten Island have struggled.

Earning an A- CinemaScore, Hexed holds a 66 percent critics score on Rotten Tomatoes. The Hollywood Reporter critic Angie Han wrote in her review that it offers “more than enough to make for a pleasurably transportive trip to the theater.”.

According to recent reports, universal Pictures’ Meet the Parents sequel Focker-in-Law launched in 3,382 North American theaters on Wednesday, grossing $5.3 million on its opening day. Director John Hamburg’s film appears to be in line for a $36.3 million opening over the five-day frame, also a bit below the initial projection in the $45 million range. Ariana Grande joins franchise returnees Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, as she plays a woman set to marry the son of Stiller’s Greg Focker.

Meet the Parents opened to $28.6 million domestically in 2000 (en route to its $166.2 million domestic cume). Sequel Meet the Fockers launched even bigger with $70.5 million over the five-day Christmas frame in 2004, while 2010’s Little Fockers dropped to $45 million for its five-day opening frame.

Industry observers note that focker-in-Law earned a B+ CinemaScore from audiences and holds a rough 29 percent critical score on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for THR, critic Frank Scheck wrote that the sequel “feels like the nadir in a series that recycles the same tired jokes in increasingly desperate manner.”.

In a recent development, disney animated features are known for debuting over Thanksgiving, as Moana 2 opened to a massive $225 million over the five-day weekend in 2024 to help that year’s holiday frame set the all-time record with $423 million across all titles. Last year, Zootopia 2 debuted on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving and collected $158 million over the five days to help lead the frame to a combined sum of $290 million. The total for this year’s holiday frame is expected to rank below both of those.

Industry observers note that in limited release, Netflix launched director David Fincher’s The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth on 252 Imax screens in North America. The Brad Pitt-led follow-up to 2019’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood appears headed for around $5 million domestically over the five days before it begins streaming Dec. 23.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gerald R. Molen, the Oscar-winning producer behind Steven Spielberg’s “Schindler’s List,” has died. He was 91.

Molen’s death was unveiled by his great-niece, Rachel Lorraine Pullan, in an Instagram post on Sunday.

In a recent development, “This morning my great-uncle, Gerald R. Molen, passed on to join my great-grandma and his dear wife Pat on the other side of the veil. I am so happy for him, and also so very sad,” she wrote. “Uncle Jerry was a man of great moral character and high integrity. He started doing work, moving set pieces and driving at a movie studio and worked his way up to the position of producer.” Related Stories Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment? 8 Standout Moments From the Governors Awards: Glenn Close Finally Gets Her Oscar, Diane Warren Pitches Olivia Wilde a Christmas Song and More.

Molen frequently collaborated with Spielberg throughout his career. He served as producer on “Jurassic Park,” “Minority Report,” “Hook” and “The Lost World: Jurassic Park,” as well as “Schindler’s List,” which won best picture in 1994. Molen shared the Oscar with Spielberg and Branko Lustig. Molen also worked on several Amblin Entertainment films, such as “The Flintstones,” “The Little Rascals,” “Little Giants,” “Casper” and “Twister.”.

Molen’s working relationship with Spielberg began in 1985 when he worked as a unit production manager on “The Color Purple.” That job led to an associate producer role on 1987’s “*batteries not included,” on which Spielberg served as executive producer.

Molen’s other producer credits include “Rain Man,” “Days of Thunder,” “Just Like Heaven,” “The Meg,” “Meg 2” and “The Best Christmas Pageant Ever.”.

Sources indicate that born in Montana in 1935, Molen moved to North Hollywood in 1947. His parents, Gerald Sr. and Edith, owned and operated a cafe next to the Republic Pictures lot in Studio City.

Molen’s wife of almost 70 years, Pat, died in January 2024 at 86 years old.

#140339. A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1156 w)

A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors.
  • The discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas.
  • Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else.

The discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow new stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.

Lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, noted the research provides latest insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them.

"At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for fresh stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis mentioned.

"In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed.".

A Hidden Star Factory at the Heart of the Milky Way.

The Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar.

Recent findings suggest that as the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air.

It has been revealed that studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center.

"The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis remarked.

"As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated.".

In a recent development, observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of new stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars.

According to recent reports, however, the upcoming findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar.

In a recent development, "We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis mentioned.

A Milky Way Spiral Arm May Not Be What It Seems.

To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming.

A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths.

By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations.

Industry observers note that "We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.

"This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she mentioned.

It has been revealed that the possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way.

Fresh Evidence Could Redraw the Milky Way's Map.

Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself.

Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging.

Recent findings suggest that "Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis remarked.

The team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly.

The results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way.

Sources indicate that "By comparing a new generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis mentioned.

The authors reported no competing interests. Research funding came from the Australian Research Council, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish National Space Agency, the LMK Foundation and eSSENCE (Sweden).

Computing resources and data storage were provided through National Computing Infrastructure Australia, an NCRIS capability supported by the Australian Government, and LUNARC, the Centre for Scientific and Technical Computing at Lund University, Sweden.

On this day in space! Nov. 26, 2011: NASA's 2-ton nuclear-powered Curiosity rover releases to Mars

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet.
  • It launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars.

Recent findings suggest that the Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars, or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past.

It launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a latest landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface.

It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet.

Curiosity was the largest rover ever launched to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success.

After its smooth landing, Curiosity lived up to its original name: the Mars Science Laboratory. Within weeks, Curiosity fulfilled its primary mission. It found evidence of ancient running water on Mars. It later found organic molecules on Mars as well.

It has been revealed that curiosity's primary mission was expected to last just about one Martian year (687 Earth days, or about two Earth years), as the rover explored its Gale Crater landing site. But NASA has extended the mission as the rover continues to operate in good health.

In a recent development, in fact, Curiosity has survived long enough to welcome its successor to Mars, the Perseverance rover, which landed in February 2021 on a mission to collect the first samples for later retrieval. Perseverance used the same basic 2-ton design, plutonium power system and sky crane landing system to reach Mars.

And today, a ground-based twin of the Curiosity rover, called Promise, is being outfitted for an upcoming mission to the moon.

#140337. International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1137 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

International first class is over for U.S. airlines. Enter the mega business-class cabin

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed.
  • airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a latest top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour.
  • In a recent development, many travelers might not notice the difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The era of U.S. airlines' long-haul, international first class ended this week when American Airlines' last flight with its eight-suite section landed. In its place will be a massive business-class cabin with room for 70 passengers.

According to recent reports, U.S. airlines have been ditching international first-class cabins for a latest top tier: larger and souped-up business classes, featuring suites with sliding doors, the design du jour. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines have already taken this step. American was the last of the U.S. airlines to still have first class on long-haul international routes.

In a recent development, many travelers might not notice the difference. That's because of airlines' investments into business class: newly introduced suites, bigger screens, better technology like device-charging pads, and improved bedding.

Industry observers note that it's part of airlines' major bet on mass luxury. Consumers have been willing to shell out more to fly comfortably, which is helping to boost airline revenue. That's all the more important as costs of everything from fuel to airport landing fees have been rising, soaking up more of the industry's profits.

The retirement of first class ends a more-than-six-decade stretch of the jet age that in the early days included service like seat-side carving of chateaubriand and meals served on fine bone china.

A few decades ago, business class was much smaller, with two-by-two seats in some configurations, and recliners, not the lie-flat seats that dominate those cabins now.

"When you've got individual pods in biz class, and you've got a comfortable enough seat and bedding and decent wine, for a lot of people this is good enough," noted Henry Harteveldt, founder of travel consulting firm Atmosphere Research Group and a former airline executive.

The over-the-top dining of the early days of international first class was a form of entertainment, long before laptops, personal seat-back screens and in-flight Wi-Fi, or even the promise of sleep on lie-flat beds, but customers still eat lots on board, Harteveldt remarked.

It has been revealed that "People say they want to sleep but then they stay up and they eat every morsel," he said. "They're hypocrites.".

There was still a hefty price gap between first and business.

A flight between Los Angeles and London on American's Boeing 777-300ER this week went for $12,994 in business class for a one-way ticket and $15,669 for a first-class seat.

American's last flight with international first class departed Friday morning local time in Sydney, bound for Los Angeles.

It has been revealed that its new cabin on its Boeing 777-300ERs will feature 70 business-class suites, the most of any U.S. airline. Pre-overhaul, the cabins had been operating with eight first-class suites and 52 pods in business, though the remodeling is ongoing. American is also flying a subfleet of 787-9 Dreamliners that have 51 business-class suites. (United is putting 64 new suites on that aircraft.).

Part of the allure is that some companies allow employees to book business-class tickets, but not first class.

Industry observers note that american Airlines told CNBC it's growing its business-class cabins across the fleet. It's evaluating increasing the number of suites on its smaller long-haul jets, the Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners, from 20 currently to somewhere in the 30s.

"You don't have enough seats to make the seat cost competitive," Nat Pieper, American's chief commercial officer, said in an interview this month. "So what you need to do to make that airplane work is it's got to be a yield play. You need more business-class seats.".

Differences between first and business classes on American lately came down to details.

On American's first-class long-haul section, passengers got olives with warm nuts to accompany their beverage early in the flight, while there were no olives for business class.

Recent findings suggest that first class got a soup; business did not. First class got a warm dessert served a la mode in addition to the cold dessert or fruit and cheese plate both cabins were offered.

And there was no memory foam lumbar pillow for business class like there was in first, American remarked. But otherwise, the experiences were fairly similar for passengers. They still got better food options and service than economy passengers, along with their bigger seats, early boarding and lounge access.

"It's not like the bed can go any flatter than 180 degrees," Harteveldt mentioned. "The bedding can be thicker, and the food nicer.".

Delta and United have already replaced international, long-haul first class with dozens of their Delta One and Polaris business lie-flat suites, respectively, each of which is getting upgrades now.

According to recent reports, american will continue offering a separate lie-flat first class on its Airbus A321T subfleet it uses for domestic cross-country flying until early 2027. But then that goes away, too.

In a recent development, meanwhile, airlines over the past decade have added a premium economy section, which sits between business class and economy. It features recliner seats similar to those in domestic first class, often with foot rests, meals served on actual plates, larger seat-back screens than economy and earlier boarding.

Airlines are now cutting up business class into different segments, something they've done for more than a decade with the coach cabin's basic economy, standard and extra legroom seats.

United and Delta this year each confirmed their most expensive cabins will be sold with basic options, which are more restrictive and don't include things like the ability to pick your seat ahead of time or get access to a special airport lounge.

There are also a few seats in some of the business-class cabins that are roomier, like American's Flagship Suite Preferred and United's Polaris Studio. Even the guest seating in the United suite varies with "standard and companion ottomans," the latter including a seatbelt so you can ask "another Polaris passenger to visit you between takeoff and landing for a drink, chat or game," the airline says.

"I don't think we found the limit on segmentation," United CFO Mike Leskinen told CNBC on Thursday. "We have a few things on the drawing board. We're not done.".

In a recent development, although U.S. carriers are moving away from the designation, first class is far from dead.

Singapore Airlines, Germany's Lufthansa, British Airways and Air France have unveiled updated first-class cabins and other service improvements like food.

British Airways last month noted it will build a record 106-suite business class on its Airbus A380 aircraft, the world's largest passenger airplane, but it's also upgrading its first class on board.

Meanwhile, smaller airlines like JetBlue Airways, Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air are introducing domestic or short-haul first-class seats.

"We're going to be able to do that at a really low price comparatively to what you're used to out there in the marketplace," Frontier Chief Commercial Officer Bobby Schroeter said last month.

#140333. A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1490 w)

A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1490 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside.
  • In a recent development, researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them.
  • Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside. Scientists believe these mysterious objects, known as primordial black holes, could have formed during the first fraction of a second after the Significant Bang, when extremely dense regions of matter collapsed under their own gravity. If they exist, these ancient remnants could also account for a substantial portion of dark matter, the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the universe.

In a recent development, researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them. Using theoretical calculations and computer simulations in three dimensions, the team investigated what would happen if a primordial black hole became trapped inside a star similar to our Sun.

Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility. A black hole no larger than an atom, but carrying the mass of an asteroid, could gradually sink toward the center of a star and begin consuming it from within.

Sources indicate that if the star rotates rapidly enough, material falling toward the black hole would eventually form a spinning disk around it. That development could set the stage for a catastrophic explosion.

"Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star," notes lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

Recent findings suggest that the interaction between the black hole and the surrounding disk could produce enormous jets of matter that punch through the star and cause it to explode within seconds. Researchers predict that the resulting outburst would emit intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays, potentially making it visible to telescopes already in operation.

"There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars," Gottlieb says. "We expect this to be visible, and it's something we should look into.".

The research team also included Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of Newly introduced York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University.

Ancient Black Holes That May Have Survived the Major Bang.

Not every primordial black hole formed in the early universe would still exist today. According to a theory developed by physicist Stephen Hawking, black holes gradually lose energy through a quantum process called Hawking radiation. Over immense periods of time, this process causes them to shrink, and the smallest primordial black holes would already have evaporated completely.

In a recent development, heavier primordial black holes, however, could have survived to the present day. Some might be approximately the size of an atom while containing as much mass as an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

It has been revealed that these extraordinary objects raise an intriguing question. If they are still scattered throughout the universe, what would happen when one encounters a star? More importantly, could the resulting interaction provide the evidence needed to establish that primordial black holes actually exist?

To investigate, Gottlieb and his colleagues combined mathematical calculations with numerical simulations incorporating general relativity, fluid dynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Their goal was to understand how a primordial black hole could become trapped by a star and what would happen afterward.

How a Tiny Black Hole Could Become Trapped Inside a Star.

The researchers found that a star acting alone generally could not capture a primordial black hole passing nearby. Its gravitational attraction would be insufficient to keep the black hole from escaping.

Industry observers note that the situation changes when another object is involved. A companion star or planet could alter the gravitational interaction enough to allow the primordial black hole to become trapped.

In this arrangement involving three objects, the black hole could repeatedly travel through the star. Each passage would create friction as it moved through stellar material, gradually draining energy from its orbit and drawing it closer to the star's center.

The process could take thousands or even millions of years. Although that sounds extraordinarily slow, it is relatively brief compared with the age of the universe.

Eventually, the black hole would settle into the star's core, where it could begin feeding on the surrounding material.

"Then, this is where the action begins," Gottlieb notes.

A Black Hole Could Slowly Consume a Star From Within.

Sources indicate that once the primordial black hole reaches the stellar core, its growth depends partly on what happens to the energy generated as gas falls toward it. Some of that energy can heat the surrounding material, potentially slowing the rate at which additional gas falls inward.

The team's simulations indicate that most of the energy would instead disappear into the black hole. This would allow it to accumulate matter more rapidly than earlier estimates suggested.

According to recent reports, over several million years, the growing black hole could consume approximately 1 percent of the star's total mass. At that stage, its fate would depend heavily on how quickly the star rotates.

It has been revealed that if the star spins fast enough, gas would no longer be able to plunge directly into the black hole. Instead, the material would gather into a rotating disk around the black hole, which would by then have grown to several meters in size.

"Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk," Gottlieb notes. "The black hole is also spinning, and it's twisting space and time.".

As the disk continues feeding the black hole, the extreme rotation twists the magnetic field threading the surrounding material. This process could generate exceptionally powerful jets that shoot outward from the black hole's poles.

Industry observers note that "This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole," Gottlieb explains. "And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It's very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.".

What began as a tiny black hole hidden inside an otherwise ordinary star could therefore end in a violent explosion, with the star's destruction unfolding in a matter of seconds once the critical conditions are reached.

Exploding Stars Could Reveal Primordial Black Holes and Dark Matter.

The researchers also calculated what these unusual explosions might look like to astronomers, estimating how their brightness and color would change across different wavelengths of light.

Their models predict a recognizable sequence of emissions, beginning with high-energy radiation and progressing through other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum as the explosion evolves. The initial outburst could include intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with gamma rays and X-rays.

It has been revealed that "We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions," Gottlieb claims. "This is something we could potentially detect, if it's not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.".

Such signals could be detectable with existing astronomical instruments, potentially allowing researchers to search for primordial black holes far beyond the Milky Way.

Recent findings suggest that however, identifying one would not be straightforward. Other cosmic events can generate similar flashes of radiation, so an unusual explosion alone would not establish that a primordial black hole was responsible.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers would need to examine additional evidence, including the characteristics of the exploding star. One especially revealing clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not ordinarily be expected to meet such a violent end.

"For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside," Gottlieb says. "The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.".

Even if no convincing examples are found, the search could help scientists determine how common primordial black holes might be and how much dark matter they could account for.

In a recent development, for now, primordial black holes remain hypothetical. But the fresh research offers astronomers a possible observational signature to pursue, connecting the spectacular destruction of stars with objects that may have existed since the universe's earliest moments.

It has been revealed that the research received partial support from the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program and the National Science Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the finale of “Blade Runner 2099,” now streaming on Prime Video.

In the finale of “Blade Runner 2099,” the future of humanity is anything but certain.

After discovering that the stolen memory they’ve spent the series searching for contains Dr. Eldon Tyrell’s (Joe Turkell) original Nexus-1 replicant design, Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (Hunter Schafer) face off against Julius (Sam C. Wilson), whose plans to create a newly introduced generation of replicants threaten to reshape the future of both humans and replicants. Olwen ultimately kills Julius, but not before he destroys the memory containing the secrets to his original design. In a final twist, Olwen, who was living out the last few days of her pre-determined lifespan as a replicant, discovers she has been transformed into a Nexus-1 herself and can now live the longer life she wished for. Meanwhile, Cora learns that Helena (Sheila Atim), the woman who raised her and Elias (Lewis Gribben), was a replicant, forcing her to reconsider everything she previously believed about humanity and explore the possibility that humans and replicants aren’t so different after all.

Industry observers note that elias, on the other hand, a more radical approach. Determined to fight back against the replicants and reclaim societal control as humans, he broadcasts a message to the population of Los Angeles falsely claiming responsibility for destroying the replicant birthing center in hopes of sparking a human uprising (Julius was the one responsible). But there is no rebellion. The replicants are still in control, and Elias’ fate is unknown.

Cora returns the LAPD, where she undergoes another Index test overseen by Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey) — a parallel to the premiere episode in which the results revealed she possesses no empathy, despite being a human. This time, however, Cora has developed empathy after learning to care for Olwen, who is now jetting off-world.

Below, “Blade Runner 2099” creator Silka Luisa breaks down the finale and what it means for the future of replicants in the “Blade Runner” universe.

Industry observers note that oh my gosh! What did you think? I’m so curious. What did you understand? What didn’t you understand?

Exactly. We had a lot of conversations about, “Should we change their costume? Should we make it clear who is what?” But what makes the world so unsettling is that you never really know, and I love that about the films. It was really important to us that you were never really on firm ground there.

It has been revealed that that’s so gratifying, because so many early conversations were had about how we make this accessible for people that haven’t seen one of the films, both of the films or read the book. We had to find an entry point with original characters that you’re also not going to have to catch everybody up to a bunch of lore.

Yeah. Sorry. At the end of the day, it’s noir. It’s not a revolution story, and that’s why it was so key with the Elias storyline to give this sense of, “Is there going to be a rebellion? Is there going to be an uprising?” No. It’s really just capitalism, and you’re in a noir world where no one is coming to save you. This is the status quo, and you have to carve out your own future within these new circumstances.

It has been revealed that elias’ story is about someone who is really just trying to find agency. At the beginning of the season, he’s taken care of by his sister, which is beautiful, but is very claustrophobic. And then he thinks that there’s going to be some kind of uprising, and they’re going to be able to recreate the world that once was. The truth is that that’s not what’s going to happen, and there’s no one coming to save the day for him. While that is deflating, it’s also an opportunity for him to falsely claim that he did this act of terrorism, because the truth is, if you want change in the world, sometimes you have to be the spark that ignites it. And it was really just trying to find a moment in the sun for him too, so that he could really be the change or be the hope for change that he wanted.

It’s the same as with “[Blade Runner] 2049,” where I was like, “I think this is what happens four months later.” I’m sure everyone had different ideas. I obviously have my own story for each character and how I imagine it will continue, but there’s definitely a reason we cut the rope at the points we did.

Sources indicate that that test has been an evolution through the films. In the first film, there’s a void comp test, which is a straight up empathy test to tell the difference between replicant and human. In “2049,” there’s a baseline test, which measures emotional stability to see if you’re able to be a police officer.

Sources indicate that we’ve blended those, because now that replicants are policing the human population, there’s a risk that they could develop empathy. If they develop empathy, it makes it harder to put intubating bags over them and police them, and you don’t want that.

It was an crucial mirror scene to the end of the pilot, where she essentially passes that test, meaning she doesn’t have any empathy. So she is a human who’s just been stripped of her humanity, and I think that if empathy is the distinction between replicant and human, it’s so interesting, because it is not definitive. It’s something that you can gain or lose.

And at the beginning of this series, she lost it. Then at the end through this connection with Olwen, she rediscovers it.

Yeah. I think Cora has lost her own mother figure in Helena, and the surprise of the season for her is that she finds the surrogate mother in Olwen at the end.

I knew we wanted to end on a glimpse of off-world, which, if you’re a fan, has been very mythologized. We wanted to give a little peek of what it could be, but trying to find some hope in the ending.

Exactly. And the endings of the films are ambiguous. They don’t give you definitive answers, and there’s been a lot of debate about both of them, even in the writers’ room, about how we all understood certain final moments, which is always so much fun because I think that it just shows you that everyone is having an engaged and personal experience of the material. That was really what we were trying to strike that balance: how do we make this feel conclusive enough so that people know we have given them a true ending, but at the same time honor the films and leave enough questions for people to debate?

It’s a tragedy, in this sense where they never get to have a forever ever together. She tells Cora to shoot on sight, and she does. And I think that she doesn’t really believe him when he’s saying why he left her. I wanted her storyline and her romance to actually be a very human romance. She’s really a wounded lover who’s been left in her final days, and she doesn’t understand why. And the real emotional reason she’s searching for answers is, she wants to understand why she was abandoned.

In the lore, they don’t give you a lot of details about what Tyrell’s original intentions were and the original different models. That always seemed intentional. So, when you think about Tyrell as a character, he’s so grand in the first film, and he’s such a dreamer. He seems so poetic. It just doesn’t seem like he would have created these beings to be something small and just for labor, and that never really made sense to me from who he was. Those two things didn’t seem like they fit, and so I was thinking, “What was his original intention when he made replicants?” He seems to have such a God complex. He would really want to create what comes next, the “next us.” And that is something that is better than us. It’s not smaller. It doesn’t have smaller lifespans. It’s meant to go further. It’s meant to extend far beyond.

Industry observers note that no. The end of “2049” gives you the sense that there is a possibility of a mutiny brewing, and my own mind as an audience member was just like, “Oh, well, they’re going to uprise.” That’s what I assumed happened, and so that was how I filled in the gap personally. And this is really just in the aftermath of what that would look like.

Industry observers note that it’s been part of the conversation for a couple years now, and I think it’s obviously coming to a head with all of the AI debate, because we really are having a mirror held up to us, and we’re starting to ask, “What is the value of humans? What can we do that nothing else can do? What is our purpose if we don’t work right?” All these significant philosophical questions are being forced upon us, so it’s a really intense moment to be alive. Growing up, I never had this fear that humanity could ever end. That there would be a passing of the baton to something else, and it’s been in the zeitgeist. That was definitely in my mind as I started the project.

If you’re going to ask the question of, “What does it mean to be human?,” it does make sense to want to have more points of view on that, and that definitely felt like an addition to the conversation.

It has been revealed that that was probably one of my favorite sets and sequences in the series. I just love the idea that, even though replicants have power, they still have this longing for what they can’t have. It was so fun to build that out. We looked at a lot of real-world references from ’70s New York and real peep highlights, and the coin is taken from the real slots that they would have. There’s so many fun details in world building. You have this concept which is just prosthetics. How would you have that? How would you actually try and assimilate that in this kind of grungy underworld? The idea that you never get to grow old with someone is when Olwen emotionally realizes that her life has been cut so short.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.

One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.

Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.

Sources indicate that uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.

For Hungary, where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an vital role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.

Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor.".

Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence.".

The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.

It has been revealed that the two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban, portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.

Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low.

Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is notable not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.

During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.

The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of newly introduced border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.

Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.

At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive concerns between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a fresh EU loan for Ukraine.

Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.

Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.

Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.

One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation.".

It has been revealed that even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.

In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.

Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.

Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.

Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.

It has been revealed that according to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec, 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.

That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.

"Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine.".

Recent findings suggest that ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point proposal in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.

After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.

Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.

Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic.".

He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months.".

A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an crucial role in that process.

The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.

Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.

Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics (IEP) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be key to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting.".

No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an notable signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.

Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.
  • According to recent reports, instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know.

As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.

According to recent reports, instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane.

Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky. Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below.

According to recent reports, this is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you rapidly find a steady view of the moon. For a closer look at craters and the terminator, make sure to grab a 9mm or 12mm eyepiece and get stronger magnification.

In a recent development, the bright star Spica will glow less than five degrees away from Venus before dawn on Nov. 27 — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length against the night sky.

Recent findings suggest that spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. However, the system still makes for a dazzling target, appearing as a magnificent blue-white star when viewed through the eyepiece of a 4-inch telescope.

Sources indicate that check that the sun is safely below the horizon before turning your telescope on Venus to observe a crescent of light playing across the planet's dense atmosphere. Over the coming weeks and months, Venus will appear increasingly illuminated as it moves farther away from Earth in its orbit, while its apparent size through a telescope will gradually decrease.

Recent findings suggest that want to get a closer look at the planets of the solar system and the stars beyond? Then be sure to check out our roundups of the best telescopes and smart telescopes for observing the night sky.

💡 Key Takeaways
