💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.
  • According to recent reports, in the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in Fresh Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds.
  • According to recent reports, resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of Latest Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming Zealanders have long envisioned the island as a predator-free zone for native birds, but swimming stoats have shown a resolve of their own.

According to recent reports, in the late 1800s, wildlife conservationists in Fresh Zealand were recognizing how predators such as stoats, brought to the country to control other nonnative animal populations, were becoming a threat to native birds. Naturalists at the time surmised that some of the nation’s islands could serve as sanctuaries where endemic species could persist, free from the voracious newcomers.

According to recent reports, resolution Island, located in the Fiordland region along the rugged southwest edge of Latest Zealand’s South Island, was one of the first eyed for this purpose. Conservationist Thomas Henry Potts proposed in 1872 that the island could be a place where “wingless species, and birds of feeble powers of flight, might there find a refuge for some of their representatives.”.

So began an early systematic effort to protect kiwi, kākāpō, and other native birds on Resolution Island, the largest of the approximately 90 islands in Fiordland National Park. This image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 on December 12, 2025, reveals the island’s setting amid a landscape of steep-sided valleys carved by glaciers and now inundated by the ocean.

Industry observers note that the uninhabited island rises from sea level to the summit of Mount Clerke at 1,069 meters (3,507 feet). Its diverse habitats and vegetation communities range from bogs and wetlands near the coast to widespread podocarp forests at middle elevations to tussock grasslands in the subalpine and alpine areas. Offshore, the Taumoana (Five Fingers Peninsula) Marine Reserve protects estuarine and wave-exposed rocky reef habitats at the entrance to Dusky Sound, east of Five Fingers Peninsula.

Farther into the sound, Pigeon Island was the onetime home of Richard Henry, who was named caretaker of Resolution Island after it was designated a reserve in 1891. In what some have called a “landmark effort,” Henry spent years transporting more than 700 birds, mostly kiwi and kākāpō, by rowboat to Resolution and other would-be island sanctuaries nearby.

In a recent development, in 1900, however, people began spotting mustelids on Resolution. It turns out the island is within swimming distance for animals such as stoats. Henry was intent on trapping the interlopers but eventually abandoned the project and moved on to caretaking work on another island. The spirit of his efforts lives on, though. A Department of Conservation program started in 2008 aims to control stoat populations and bolster native species on Resolution.

NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stretching over 200,000 square kilometers across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world’s largest regions of limestone.
  • Ultimately, this led to the familiar dry landscape of today, which has acted as a significant barrier for plants, animals, and poorly adapted colonial Victorian-era explorers who described it as “the sort of place one gets into in bad dreams”.
  • In contrast, the Mirning People of the Nullarbor and Great Australian Bight have lived for tens of thousands of years on this southern margin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stretching over 200,000 square kilometers across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world’s largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago.

Ultimately, this led to the familiar dry landscape of today, which has acted as a significant barrier for plants, animals, and poorly adapted colonial Victorian-era explorers who described it as “the sort of place one gets into in bad dreams”.

In contrast, the Mirning People of the Nullarbor and Great Australian Bight have lived for tens of thousands of years on this southern margin. They have watched the landscapes change and sea levels fall and rise with the build-up and collapse of the last ice age about 20,000 years ago.

Sources indicate that to an untrained eye the Nullarbor Plain appears deceptively simple and featureless. However, beneath the immense plain lies a remarkable, largely hidden underground world.

According to recent reports, over millions of years, water has eaten away at the limestone and created complex cave networks that can extend for kilometers underground. Sadly, the caves remain poorly understood, partly because they’re only really known and accessible where they breach the surface.

Our latest study, published in Communications Earth & Environment, reveals a new way to track these cave systems even when they are deeply buried. Our work helps explain the formation of previously mysterious, shallow trench features on the Nullarbor. It also provides a new way to identify hidden caves elsewhere – even beyond our own planet.

Scattered across the Nullarbor are tell-tale signs of its vulnerability to being dissolved – small cave openings and shallow depressions.

But there are also structures of previously unknown origin and significance: long (up to 20 km), shallow (a few meters) trenches that trend roughly north-south. They’re almost invisible from the ground, but we can clearly see them in modern digital landscape models.

These shallow trenches look somewhat like flat-bottomed valleys, but they were not carved by rivers. They begin and end abruptly and are not connected to existing rivers or drainage networks that extend into the upland areas around the Nullarbor.

They also lack typical river branching patterns and the sediments within them don’t show any evidence of being deposited from flowing water.

To understand how these strange structures formed, we combined several investigative techniques.

First, we mapped the trenches using drone and aerial photography, as well as detailed satellite-based digital landscape models. Then the layers of soil and rock were measured in boreholes and caves.

Finally, we used specialized geophysical techniques to “see” inside the Earth, somewhat similar to the way an X-ray enables us to see our internal body structures from the outside.

The work demonstrated that the shallow surface trenches sit above deep zones of broken rock, and in places line up with known cave systems and sinkholes.

This means the trenches are mere muted surface expressions of deeply buried cave systems. These systems are slowly, over millions of years, “collapsing upwards” through the overlying rock layers to reach the surface.

Sources indicate that the results of this work will change how scientists interpret cave landscapes globally. It demonstrates that to explain the surface structures we see, we must look deeper than we might think.

Understanding where voids may exist underground can be key for planning both surface (buildings, roads) and subsurface (tunnels, sewers) engineering works, mitigating geological hazards, and accessing and protecting groundwater resources.

Pockmarked karst landscapes (where rocks are dissolved by water, resulting in caves and sinkholes) represent 15% of the ice-free Earth’s surface and supply water to 10–25% of the global population.

It has been revealed that more fundamentally, caves are key scientific archives. Because caves are sheltered from surface weathering and erosion processes, they can preserve snapshots of ancient environments and ecosystems that would otherwise be lost to time.

Furthermore, they may host an array of strange and vulnerable life-forms that have evolved and adapted in isolation. These are some of the least studied organisms on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that to learn more, we must first locate the cave structures. And the results of our study could be very important in this regard.

According to recent reports, the implications of this new work even extend beyond our own planet. Because caves offer a stable environment and shelter from damaging space radiation, they provide promising exploration sites for life on other planets.

Mapping of planetary surfaces within our Solar System has identified numerous potential caves, including some thought to be related to karst on Mars.

In a recent development, the Nullarbor’s dry, stable surface is an excellent analogue to help locate the subtle surface fingerprints of hidden cave systems on planets that now lack a dynamic water-cycle – such as Mars. Even if the caves are barren of life, they could be attractive bases for future human explorers.

Recent findings suggest that how many other apparently simple landscapes around the world or on other planets are concealing large cave systems underneath? We don’t yet know, but the trenches we studied are unlikely to be unique. Similar subtle landforms are likely to have been overlooked elsewhere, too.

Sometimes the most remarkable discoveries are waiting in understated but plain view, in landscapes we think we already understand.

Webb from La Trobe University; Uroš Stepišnik, Matej Dolenec, Primož Miklavc, Tomislav Popit and Andrej Šmuc from the University of Ljubljana; and Jian-xin Zhao from The University of Queensland.

#140235. What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate?

What is the US permitting bill and would it actually help the climate?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The dust has barely settled on the Democrats' massive midterm showing, but lawmakers still have business to get done before a newly introduced US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.
  • Permitting reform might sound like a snooze.
  • BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dust has barely settled on the Democrats' massive midterm showing, but lawmakers still have business to get done before a newly introduced US Congress takes office in 2027: namely, a permitting reform bill with rare cross-party support that could accelerate clean energy or fossil fuels — or both, depending on who's asked.

Permitting reform might sound like a snooze. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) could have far-reaching consequences for the country's energy mix, household utility bills and climate goals.

BAAJA, which is backed by US President Donald Trump, has already cleared the Senate and now faces a vote in the House of Representatives. DW breaks down what's in the bill, the political fight playing out on the sidelines and what it could mean for consumers' wallets and the US energy transition.

Before many new solar farms, wind projects or power plants can connect to the electricity grid, they must first pass through an arduous and complex permitting process.

Recent findings suggest that getting the green light for an energy project can often take years and requires permits from multiple government agencies. If it manages to overcome those hurdles, a legal challenge can easily stop upcoming infrastructure in its tracks.

It has been revealed that the nearly 500-page bill aims to overhaul that process. It would speed up environmental reviews, simplify the planning and construction of power transmission lines, make permits harder to revoke and require the growing number of data centers to pay for any needed grid upgrades.

The bill is mostly technology agnostic. So, the same reforms that would make it easier to build a lot of green energy infrastructure promptly could, in theory, be used to speed up oil and gas projects whose carbon emissions are warming the planet.

That's what's made BAAJA controversial, with some Democrats saying permitting reform is needed to get energy bills down and others saying they support provisions, like building more transmission lines required for transporting green energy, but not the whole package.

It's hard to estimate, and there's a lot of contradictory information out there.

Recent findings suggest that the Rhodium Group, an independent research firm, found the bill would lower US greenhouse gas emissions in every scenario it ran, by up to 4% in 2040 compared with no bill. This is a fraction of the emissions reductions targets the US dropped when it withdrew from Paris climate accord this year.

Purdue University engineer Kevin Kircher reached the opposite conclusion. His analysis, which has not been peer-reviewed, estimates that domestic emissions would rise by about 2%, mostly because he assumes the bill would boost US fossil fuel production.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that the difference comes down to a bet about what the bill ends up accelerating more: renewables and the power lines to carry them, or fossil fuels. That depends on which administration is issuing the permits.

Sources indicate that under the administration of former President Joe Biden, for instance, renewables got a boost. But since Trump took office in January 2025, his administration has favored fossil fuels and spent billions paying developers to give up their offshore wind leases.

The White House Council of Economic Advisers, a team of economists that advises the president, has estimated the measure would eventually cut the average household electricity bill by $178 to $251 (€162 to €229) a year.

Sources indicate that the logic is that long permitting delays discourage investment in infrastructure, which drives up prices. But that estimate considers only one part of the bill, faster environmental reviews, and doesn't say when the savings would arrive.

In a recent development, independent analyses also found a drop in electricity prices for consumers, though a more modest one. The Rhodium Group estimated the bill's passage would save the average household $41 to $66 a year by 2035. That's largely because upcoming transmission lines would let cheaper power reach customers, and the costs of expanding the grid for data centers would no longer be passed on to households.

Critics have pointed to the fact that those savings are relative. Electricity demand from data centers is expected to push up prices regardless, and permitting reform would only slow that rise rather than reverse it.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Oil Change International, an advocacy group that opposes the bill, argues households will still end up paying more for energy than they do now, especially if the bill mainly speeds up gas projects, since US gas prices are expected to rise sharply over the next decade.

It has been revealed that most major US environmental groups oppose the bill as written, including the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Earthjustice. The Sierra Club called it "fundamentally flawed.".

Much of the criticism focuses on provisions making federal permits harder to revoke.

"It would prevent a future administration from reconsidering a prior administration's flawed decisions to authorize activities such as Arctic drilling, deep seabed mining, or development of data centers on public lands," Earthjustice wrote in a critique.

It has been revealed that the reverse is also true. That provision also makes it harder for an administration to come in and halt clean energy projects, as Trump did with offshore wind.

In a recent development, opponents have warned the bill could weaken protection for water and habitats, and limit environmental lawsuits. One area that environmental groups have praised is the overhaul of how transmission lines are planned and approved.

That matters, because the windiest and sunniest places in the US are often far from the cities that need power, and building long-distance power lines to connect them can take a decade or more.

Still, many critics say they would rather wait until Democrats control Congress in January and pass a version more focused on clean energy. Though that approach is risky, any bill would still require Trump's signature to become law.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Sources indicate that explanation: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder. And there is much to behold in today's featured image. The Milky Way shines bright in the sky of Brazil, over the white sand dunes and dark lagoons of Lençóis Maranhenses National Park. We can see different parts of the Milky Way as it apparently rotates in the sky every night and throughout the year. This composite image was taken later in the night in July from a latitude of approximately 2º south. It demonstrates some prominent Milky Way features, such as dark dust lanes and colorful nebulas. But does the Galaxy really appear arched like a rainbow in the sky? No, this is an artifact of a picture taken with a wide-angle lens. As the Galaxy was artfully framed by the photographer, it matches the contour of the dark lagoon creating the illusion of a cosmic eye, half in space and half on the ground. Is this eye in the sky looking back at you?Tomorrow's picture: what's next?

Industry News: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that more than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea.
  • In a recent development, the discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX.
  • "Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that more than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea. These unusually salty underwater lakes could provide clues to how Earth's oceans formed millions of years ago and help guide the search for life on other planets.

In a recent development, the discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX. The researchers located the pools at a depth of more than one mile (1,770 meters) using a remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) deployed from the OceanXplorer, an advanced research vessel equipped to investigate some of the least accessible environments on Earth.

"Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis. "Our discovery of a rich community of microbes that survive in extreme environments can help trace the limits of life on Earth and can be applied to the search for life elsewhere in our solar system and beyond.".

Life thrives in extreme underwater lakes.

According to recent reports, brine pools rank among the harshest environments on our planet. Their waters contain exceptionally high concentrations of salt, feature unusual chemical conditions, and are completely devoid of oxygen. Despite these seemingly inhospitable conditions, the pools support abundant microbial life. Previous research on microbes inhabiting Red Sea brine pools has even identified biologically active molecules with potential anticancer properties.

The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, mark the first documented discovery of brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba. Remarkably, the researchers nearly missed them.

Industry observers note that "We were very lucky," noted Purkis. "The discovery came in the last five minutes of the ten-hour ROV dive that we could dedicate to this project.".

Hidden records of ancient tsunamis and earthquakes.

Beyond their biological significance, the pools serve as natural archives of the region's geological history. Situated relatively close to the coastline, their extremely salty waters and absence of oxygen help preserve evidence of tsunamis, flash floods, and earthquakes that occurred in the Gulf of Aqaba thousands of years ago. Regional tectonic activity has produced numerous faults and fractures across the seabed in this part of the gulf.

According to recent reports, earlier in 2022, Purkis and his colleagues uncovered evidence of a 500-year-old underwater landslide that likely generated a substantial tsunami. Understanding the region's history of such events could have important implications for coastal development in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

The study, titled "Discovery of the deep-sea NEOM Brine Pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea," was published on June 27, 2022, in Communications Earth & Environment.

Recent findings suggest that the research team included Sam J. Purkis, Hannah Shernisky, Peter K. Swart, Arash Sharifi, Amanda Oehlert, Gaëlle Duchâtellier, James Klaus, Gregor P. Eberli, Larry Peterson, and Graham Kolodziej from the UM Rosenstiel School; Fabio Marchese and Francesca Benzoni from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology's Red Sea Research Center; Giovanni Chimienti from the University of Bari Aldo Moro in Italy; Andrew Craig and Mattie Rodrigue from OceanX; Jürgen Titschack from MARUM -- Center for Marine Environmental Sciences in Germany; and Ameer Abdulla from NEOM.

NEOM, a tech giant developing the Saudi Arabian coastline, provided funding for the four-week research expedition aboard the OceanXplorer.

Watch the NEOM OceanX documentary about the discovery: https://youtu.be/bWNftnYDx9c.

Sources indicate that materials provided by University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#140229. Industry News: A newly introduced approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine indicates early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1480 w)

Industry News: A newly introduced approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine indicates early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

Industry observers note that china and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

According to recent reports, as long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

Sources indicate that the immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler remarked.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with latest variants.

Industry observers note that the new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

“You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler stated.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

It has been revealed that as promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

Recent findings suggest that “They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the new research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an enhancement.

Industry observers note that it also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler says they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

It has been revealed that other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a new vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

It has been revealed that in reality, Poland stated, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

Recent findings suggest that “That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he said.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax indicates it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Sources indicate that another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a manufacturer called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very important in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler remarked.

They have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

According to recent reports, fluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.

The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The tech giant remarked that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.

Sources indicate that "We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about.".

Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.

The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.

Bonfig said the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game releases and a targeted product assortment.

Looking ahead into the holiday season, he stated the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.

"We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more upcoming customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig noted. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year.".

Here's how the organization performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

In a recent development, best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.

Recent findings suggest that revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.

Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs.

Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.

Bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a new gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.

"I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.

#140225. The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (746 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

The surprising reason women seem better at multitasking than men

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, men and women appear to be similarly skilled at juggling multiple activities, but fresh research has uncovered one striking difference.
  • It has been revealed that whether driving, working, doing household chores, or enjoying leisure activities, people frequently find themselves managing several tasks at once or switching between them.
  • With support from the Bial Foundation, researchers André and Diana Szameitat (from Brunel University of London and City St George's, University of London, UK, respectively) set out to determine whether meaningful differences exist in multitasking ability and what might explain the widespread belief that women have an advantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, men and women appear to be similarly skilled at juggling multiple activities, but fresh research has uncovered one striking difference. In an experiment designed to recreate the demands of everyday life, men ignored conversational questions more than twice as often as women while performing just as well on the other tasks.

It has been revealed that whether driving, working, doing household chores, or enjoying leisure activities, people frequently find themselves managing several tasks at once or switching between them. Although women are widely believed to be better at multitasking than men, previous research has found only minor and inconsistent differences between the sexes, raising doubts about the accuracy of this popular assumption.

With support from the Bial Foundation, researchers André and Diana Szameitat (from Brunel University of London and City St George's, University of London, UK, respectively) set out to determine whether meaningful differences exist in multitasking ability and what might explain the widespread belief that women have an advantage.

Putting Multitasking Skills to the Test.

In a recent development, in their study, "Men Talk Less Than Women During Multitasking," published in the scientific journal Psychological Research, the researchers developed an experiment involving five different activities. The setup was designed to capture the complexity of everyday multitasking more accurately than most previous studies.

The first experiment involved 41 men and 37 women. Participants were asked to follow a recipe in a kitchen setting, look up phone numbers, match numbers with letters, watch a slideshow for specific words, and answer conversational questions. A fresh question was posed every 20 seconds (e.g., "Would you rather lose all of your money and valuables or all of the pictures you have ever taken, and why?").

In a second experiment, the researchers recruited 160 observers to determine whether differences in multitasking behavior were noticeable to others. Without being given prior information about the participants or findings, the observers watched video recordings of the experiments and assessed how well the participants performed.

One Surprising Difference Between Men and Women.

Men and women achieved comparable results on four of the five activities. Conversation, however, revealed a notable exception. Men left conversational questions unanswered more than twice as often as women. When men did answer, their responses were just as fast and of comparable quality to those given by women.

Industry observers note that the researchers suggest that women may, on average, be more inclined to engage in communication during social interactions. However, the study did not directly investigate this possibility, so the explanation should be treated with caution. The results are also consistent with evolutionary theories suggesting that women may have a greater tendency to engage in conversation.

How Conversation Shapes Perceptions of Ability.

The differences in conversational engagement appeared to have a considerable impact on how others judged the participants. Observers rated men as having less control over the activities, performing more poorly, putting in less effort, and being less alert than women. They also perceived men as less happy and as deriving less enjoyment from the experience.

Rather than revealing a broad difference in multitasking ability between men and women, the research points to a much more specific behavioral distinction: men are more likely to leave conversations unanswered when managing several activities simultaneously.

Sources indicate that because conversational engagement is easily noticed by others, this difference may create the impression that men are less effective at multitasking, even when their performance on other activities is comparable to that of women. The findings offer a potential explanation for how the popular stereotype that women are better multitaskers developed and why it continues to persist.

In a recent development, "Taken together, our data confirm that there are no substantial sex differences in cognitive visual-manual tasks, but that significant sex differences do exist in the ability to hold a conversation while multitasking," explains André Szameitat. This is "an ability highly salient in everyday life and, thus, could explain the development of the widespread public stereotype that women are better at multitasking than men," the researcher concludes.

Tech Report: Octopuses Use a Multi-Step Process to Squeeze Into Tiny Spaces

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, squeezing your body into the tiniest possible space is no easy task, but it can be very useful, especially if you’re a soft-bodied creature living in the fiercely competitive ocean.
  • In a recent study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers uncovered the process octopuses go through to squish themselves into small spaces.
  • The research team set up a tank divided by a transparent acrylic panel with a hole in it, allowing the octopus to move through the hole to the other side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, squeezing your body into the tiniest possible space is no easy task, but it can be very useful, especially if you’re a soft-bodied creature living in the fiercely competitive ocean. Octopuses are the masters of this kind of contortion, being able to squeeze through just about any opening wider than their beaks. Not only is it an impressive feat, but scientists are interested in this ability because it could aid in the design of biologically inspired robots.

In a recent study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers uncovered the process octopuses go through to squish themselves into small spaces. Before this, “there [was] no information about how octopuses squeeze through an opening far smaller than the body diameter,” Wen-Tzu Hsing, first author of the study, said in a press release.

The research team set up a tank divided by a transparent acrylic panel with a hole in it, allowing the octopus to move through the hole to the other side. They classified the openings as large or small depending on whether the octopuses would have to squish the stiff cartilage structure that protects their central nervous systems, which the researchers could estimate by measuring the distance between their eyes.

What surprised the scientists was the slightly different approaches octopuses used when moving through gaps of different sizes. When the gap was on the larger side, the process involved three distinct steps. First, the creatures would explore the hole with their arms. They’d then usually insert two arms through to the other side before threading their other arms and mantle through the hole. Often, this final step involved suckering the arms that led the way to the barrier for increased leverage.

Sources indicate that however, when the holes got smaller, the octopuses opted for a four-step process instead. The process was the same up to the second stage—where several arms were threaded through the opening—but the subsequent movements differed slightly. For a smaller opening, the octopus would rotate its body upward and push the bases of the arms that had already passed through deeper into the hole to widen the passage. From that position, it twisted and stretched its arms to feed all of them through. Then, once all appendages were on the other side, the octopus slid its head through, also using its tentacles on the barrier for leverage.

In the 30 successful attempts to pass through the hole observed in this experiment, the octopuses never used this four-step sequence when presented with the large hole. Additionally, side-view footage confirmed that during the last step of moving through a small opening, the octopus deforms its mantle to reduce its diameter. The octopuses also had a preference for which arms they used for the various steps.

These experiments were conducted with juveniles from two species, the common octopus and the Maya octopus. The researchers therefore don’t know whether these processes hold true across other octopus species, but beyond the strictly biological world, the researchers suggest that these findings could be useful for the design and control of soft robots.

Recent findings suggest that in environments where the size of passageways cannot be predicted—such as among debris at disaster sites—robots used for search and rescue must be designed to fit through the narrowest passages. Consequently, many existing robots adopt a long, slender, snake-like shape; however, miniaturization inevitably comes at the expense of sensors and operational capabilities. The research team hopes to apply the insights gained from the octopus in this experiment to the control of soft robots designed to search disaster debris or explore difficult terrain.

This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel capzized off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities noted on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, remarked in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it capsized about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

It has been revealed that according to Spanish authorities, the Med Emre was drifting upside down northwest of Ibiza after capsizing. Initially, they said the ship had sunk to the seabed in 1,000 metres of water, but later corrected this statement.

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the incident was not immediately clear.

The Transport Ministry said the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable.".

But he stated the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood.".

It has been revealed that "It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.

Industry observers note that spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR: On Black Friday (Nov. 27), the first 100 guests in line at every Target store get a free $25, $50, or $100 Target gift card — plus one $1,000 winner per store (no purchase necessary).

According to recent reports, target is giving early birds a major incentive to set their alarms on Black Friday morning. On Friday, Nov. 27, the retailer is handing out free Target gift cards worth $25, $50, or $100 to the first 100 eligible guests in line at every store — plus one lucky shopper at each location will walk away with a $1,000 Target gift card.

Unlike online doorbusters that disappear in seconds, this giveaway happens strictly in person and comes with a tight arrival and redemption window.

Recent findings suggest that target stores reopen at 6 a.m. local time on Black Friday, Nov. 27. Showing up right at 6 a.m. will be too late if you want a free gift card. Target associates will start handing out prize redemption tickets to the first 100 eligible people in line roughly an hour before doors open (around 5 a.m. local time at most stores).

Tickets are handed out on a first-come, first-served basis while supplies last, with a strict limit of one ticket per person.

Once doors open at 6 a.m. local time, you have to take your ticket to the Black Friday event cart inside that same Target store within one hour of store opening (by 7 a.m. local time at 6 a.m. locations). If you miss that one-hour redemption window, you forfeit your prize.

It has been revealed that your card's exact dollar value is revealed when you redeem your ticket at the event cart. Out of the 100 winners at every store, 60 people get a $25 gift card, 30 get a $50 gift card, nine get a $100 gift card, and one person gets the $1,000 grand prize.

The giveaway is open to shoppers ages 13 and older (minors need a parent or legal guardian's permission to participate), and no purchase is necessary to get a ticket or claim a card.

Once you claim your gift card, you can spend it right away on Target's Black Friday sale or save it for later in stores and online — just note that you cannot use it on prepaid or specialty gift cards. Anything you buy that's eligible also qualifies for Target's Holiday Price Match Guarantee through Dec. 24.

Double-check your local Target's exact hours before heading out — and if you are mapping out a multi-store morning route, check out our guide to Black Friday 2026 store hours to see when other major retailers open their doors.
